choices.explanation: The split of responsibilities is not fixed or equal; it shifts depending on the service model (IaaS, PaaS, SaaS). There is no fixed 50/50 division.

questions.tip: Think about which security concerns belong to the physical and virtualization layer versus which concerns belong to the workload running on top.
questions.explanation:
The shared responsibility model divides security obligations into two categories. AWS secures the infrastructure that runs all AWS services (physical facilities, hardware, hypervisor, and global network). Customers are responsible for everything they place on top of that infrastructure, including their data, identity and access configuration, network controls, and operating-system settings.

**Why it works:** The model cleanly separates what AWS controls (the physical and virtualization layer) from what the customer controls (their workloads and configurations), ensuring both parties understand their obligations.

**Why the others don't work:**
- AWS managing everything end-to-end: AWS never owns the customer's OS, application, or data layers.
- Customers owning physical security: Data center and network fabric security is exclusively AWS's responsibility.
- Fixed 50/50 split: Responsibility boundaries shift based on the service consumed, not a fixed ratio.

skills: 2.1.1: Recognizing the components of the AWS shared responsibility model.
questions.question: Match each component of the AWS environment to the party responsible for securing it under the shared responsibility model.

slots.label: Physical data center security
Guest operating system patches on Amazon EC2
Hypervisor and virtualization layer
IAM user permissions and access policies

choices.text: AWS
choices.explanation: AWS owns the physical and virtualization infrastructure, including data centers and the hypervisor layer.

choices.text: Customer
choices.explanation: Customers own their guest OS configuration, application code, and identity/access management settings.

questions.tip: Consider whether the component exists below or above the virtualization boundary that AWS manages.
questions.explanation: Under the shared responsibility model, AWS owns everything from the physical layer up to and including the hypervisor. Customers own everything they configure on top: guest operating systems, applications, and access control policies. Physical data center security and the hypervisor are 'security of the cloud' (AWS). EC2 guest OS patching and IAM policy management are 'security in the cloud' (customer).

skills: 2.1.2: Describing the customer's responsibilities on AWS.
questions.question:
You are a cloud architect reviewing the security posture of your organization's AWS environment. The team stores sensitive customer records in Amazon S3 buckets and uses AWS IAM to control access.

Which TWO items are the customer's responsibility to secure in this environment? (Select TWO)

choices.text: Configuring Amazon S3 bucket policies and access control lists to restrict who can read or write objects.
choices.explanation: Bucket policies and ACLs are customer-managed access controls. Configuring them correctly is entirely the customer's responsibility.

choices.text: Ensuring that IAM roles and user permissions follow the principle of least privilege.
choices.explanation: IAM identity and permission management is a core customer responsibility. AWS provides the IAM service, but customers define and maintain all permission boundaries.

choices.text: Encrypting the physical storage media on which Amazon S3 data is stored in AWS data centers.
choices.explanation: Physical storage media and the encryption of that media at the hardware level is AWS's responsibility. Customers manage encryption at the object or server-side encryption policy level.

choices.text: Managing the global network backbone that routes requests between AWS Regions.
choices.explanation: The global AWS network backbone is infrastructure that AWS builds and operates. It is outside the customer's responsibility boundary.

choices.text: Maintaining the availability of the Amazon S3 service endpoints across AWS Availability Zones.
choices.explanation: Service endpoint availability is AWS's responsibility. Customers use the endpoints but do not manage their availability or redundancy.

questions.tip: Identify what the customer directly configures versus what AWS manages as part of the underlying service infrastructure.
questions.explanation:
Customers are responsible for the logical security of their AWS resources. For Amazon S3, this includes controlling who can access objects via bucket policies and ACLs. For AWS IAM, this means defining permissions and ensuring they follow least-privilege principles. AWS handles the physical infrastructure, global network, and service availability.

**Why it works:** Bucket policies and IAM permissions are directly configurable by the customer and represent the customer's primary access-control obligations.

**Why the others don't work:**
- Physical media encryption: AWS manages hardware-level encryption for storage media.
- Global network backbone: AWS designs and operates its own global network.
- S3 endpoint availability: Service availability across Availability Zones is an AWS responsibility.

skills: 2.1.2: Describing the customer's responsibilities on AWS.
questions.question: A team is launching a new Amazon EC2 instance to host a web application. Arrange the following customer security responsibilities in the correct order, from the broadest foundational step to the most application-specific step.

choices.text: Create and assign an IAM role with least-privilege permissions to the EC2 instance.
choices.explanation: Establishing identity and access controls for the instance is a foundational step that governs what AWS services the workload can interact with.

choices.text: Configure security group rules to restrict inbound and outbound network traffic to only required ports.
choices.explanation: Network-level controls are applied next to define the traffic boundary around the instance before the OS is hardened.

choices.text: Apply the latest operating system patches and security updates to the guest instance.
choices.explanation: OS patching hardens the guest environment after the network boundary is in place, reducing the attack surface before the application is deployed.

choices.text: Enable application-level encryption for data the web application stores and transmits.
choices.explanation: Application-layer encryption is the most granular responsibility and is configured last, after the identity, network, and OS layers are secured.

questions.tip: Consider which security layer each step addresses and how each layer depends on the one beneath it.
questions.explanation: Customer security responsibilities for an EC2-hosted workload follow a layered approach. Identity and access controls define what the workload can do at the AWS API level. Network controls restrict traffic at the perimeter. OS patching hardens the guest environment. Application-level encryption protects data at its most specific layer. Each layer builds on the one before it.

skills: 2.1.3: Describing AWS responsibilities.
questions.question:
The engineering team is evaluating whether to use Amazon RDS for a new relational database workload. A developer asks what database-level tasks AWS handles automatically so the team can focus their effort on application logic.

Which task does AWS perform as part of its responsibilities when a customer uses Amazon RDS?

choices.text: Patching the underlying database engine software and the operating system on the managed RDS instance.
choices.explanation: For managed services like Amazon RDS, AWS takes over OS and database engine patching. This is one of the key managed-service benefits and represents AWS's responsibility for the underlying software stack.

choices.text: Designing the database schema and determining which tables require row-level security.
choices.explanation: Schema design and application-level security decisions are the customer's responsibility. AWS does not define how data is organized or protected at the application level.

choices.text: Creating database user accounts and setting passwords that comply with the organization's password policy.
choices.explanation: Database user management, including account creation and password policies within the database engine, remains a customer responsibility even on Amazon RDS.

choices.text: Configuring the Amazon RDS parameter group settings to optimize query performance for the workload.
choices.explanation: RDS parameter group configuration is a customer responsibility. Customers tune engine parameters to match their performance requirements.

questions.tip: Consider which tasks AWS automates to reduce operational overhead on managed database services versus what the customer still controls.
questions.explanation:
On managed services like Amazon RDS, AWS extends its responsibilities beyond physical infrastructure to include the managed software layers: the underlying OS and the database engine itself. AWS patches both automatically, removing that burden from customers. Customers retain responsibility for database design, user management, parameter tuning, and data access controls.

**Why it works:** OS and engine patching is explicitly called out as an AWS responsibility for managed services, distinguishing RDS from an EC2-hosted self-managed database.

**Why the others don't work:**
- Schema design and row-level security: Application-level decisions are always the customer's domain.
- Database user accounts: User management within the DB engine is a customer task on RDS.
- Parameter group configuration: Performance tuning through parameter groups is customer-controlled.

skills: 2.1.3: Describing AWS responsibilities.
questions.question: Match each security or operational task to the party responsible for it under the AWS shared responsibility model.

slots.label: Replacing failed hard drives in an AWS data center
Patching the Amazon RDS database engine
Configuring Amazon S3 bucket versioning
Managing the global AWS network backbone

choices.text: AWS
choices.explanation: Physical hardware maintenance, managed-service engine patching, and global network operations are all AWS responsibilities.

choices.text: Customer
choices.explanation: Feature configuration within AWS services, such as enabling S3 versioning, is always the customer's choice and responsibility.

questions.tip: Consider whether the task involves the underlying infrastructure AWS operates or a configuration decision within a service the customer uses.
questions.explanation: AWS is responsible for the physical infrastructure (hard drive replacement, data center operations), the global network, and the managed software layers of PaaS services (RDS engine patching). Customers are responsible for the configuration choices they make within AWS services, such as enabling versioning on Amazon S3. Turning on a service feature is a customer action, not something AWS does automatically on the customer's behalf.

skills: 2.1.4: Describing responsibilities that the customer and AWS share.
questions.question:
The security team at a healthcare company is preparing for a compliance audit and wants to document which controls are jointly exercised by both the organization and AWS. The workloads run on Amazon EC2 instances in a Virtual Private Cloud.

Which aspect of security is BEST described as a shared responsibility between AWS and the customer?

choices.text: Configuration management, where AWS maintains secure configurations for the infrastructure layer and customers maintain secure configurations for their operating systems and applications.
choices.explanation: Configuration management spans both sides of the model. AWS owns the configuration of the underlying infrastructure, and customers own the configuration of everything they deploy. Both parties apply configuration management within their respective domains.

choices.text: Physical access to servers, which both AWS and the customer control by sharing data center entry credentials.
choices.explanation: Physical server access is exclusively AWS's responsibility. Customers are never granted physical access to AWS data centers or server hardware.

choices.text: Encryption key rotation for AWS-managed encryption keys stored in AWS KMS, which AWS and the customer alternate on a fixed schedule.
choices.explanation: AWS-managed keys are rotated by AWS; customer-managed keys are rotated by the customer. These responsibilities do not alternate on a shared schedule.

choices.text: Customer data classification, which AWS performs automatically and the customer refines using tags.
choices.explanation: Data classification is entirely the customer's responsibility. AWS does not classify customer data; tagging is a customer-initiated action.

questions.tip: Look for categories of security practice that both parties must apply independently within their own domains.
questions.explanation:
Configuration management is a well-recognized shared responsibility. AWS must configure the infrastructure it manages securely (servers, hypervisors, global network). Customers must configure the resources they deploy securely (EC2 instance hardening, application settings, security group rules). Both parties exercise this control type, but over different layers. Patch management and awareness and training are similarly structured shared responsibilities.

**Why it works:** Configuration management is explicitly listed by AWS as a shared control, applied by each party within its own domain.

**Why the others don't work:**
- Physical access: This is solely AWS's domain; customers never access AWS physical hardware.
- KMS key rotation on a shared schedule: AWS-managed and customer-managed keys have distinct rotation responsibilities, not a shared alternating schedule.
- Data classification by AWS: Customers are solely responsible for classifying and tagging their own data.

skills: 2.1.4: Describing responsibilities that the customer and AWS share.
questions.question:
To reduce infrastructure costs, the organization is consolidating its AWS security documentation and wants to identify which controls must be exercised by both AWS and the customer, each within their own domain. The workloads run on Amazon EC2 with AWS Config enabled for compliance tracking.

Which TWO controls are examples of shared responsibilities that both AWS and the customer apply independently within their respective layers?

choices.text: Patch management, where AWS patches the infrastructure and hypervisor, and the customer patches the guest operating system and installed software.
choices.explanation: Patch management is a shared control. AWS patches the underlying infrastructure; customers patch their own guest OS and applications. Each party applies the control independently.

choices.text: Configuration management, where AWS maintains secure baseline configurations for infrastructure services and customers maintain secure configurations for their EC2 instances and applications.
choices.explanation: Configuration management is explicitly listed as a shared control. AWS enforces secure configurations on the underlying hardware and services; customers enforce secure configurations on their own workloads.

choices.text: Physical perimeter security of AWS data centers, which both AWS and the customer monitor through shared access to data center security feeds.
choices.explanation: Physical perimeter security is exclusively AWS's responsibility. Customers do not monitor or access data center security feeds.

choices.text: Global network capacity planning, which AWS performs at the infrastructure level while customers allocate bandwidth on a shared quota system.
choices.explanation: Global network capacity planning is an AWS infrastructure responsibility. Customers do not participate in capacity decisions for the AWS global network.

choices.text: Setting the root account password for the AWS management console, a task both AWS and the customer perform using a split-knowledge approach.
choices.explanation: The root account password belongs entirely to the customer. AWS does not set, store, or co-manage the customer's root credentials.

questions.tip: Consider which types of security practice can be meaningfully applied to both an infrastructure layer and a workload layer independently.
questions.explanation:
AWS classifies certain controls as 'inherited controls' (AWS's alone), 'customer-specific controls' (customer's alone), and 'shared controls' that both parties exercise within their own domain. Patch management and configuration management are the two most cited shared controls. AWS patches the infrastructure; customers patch their EC2 instances. AWS configures the underlying services securely; customers configure their deployments securely.

**Why it works:** Both patch management and configuration management require effort from both parties at different layers of the stack.

**Why the others don't work:**
- Physical perimeter security: Exclusively AWS's domain; customers have no access.
- Global network capacity planning: An AWS infrastructure function; customers do not share in this responsibility.
- Root account password management: This is entirely the customer's responsibility; AWS never manages customer credentials.

skills: 2.1.5: Describing how AWS responsibilities and customer responsibilities can shift, depending on the service used (for example, Amazon RDS, AWS Lambda, Amazon EC2).
questions.question:
After reviewing quarterly spending, the engineering team decides to refactor a batch processing application from Amazon EC2 to AWS Lambda to reduce costs. A security engineer wants to confirm how their security responsibilities change with this migration.

Compared to running the batch processor on Amazon EC2, what additional responsibility does AWS take on when the workload is moved to AWS Lambda?

choices.text: Managing and patching the underlying execution environment, including the operating system and runtime, that runs the Lambda function code.
choices.explanation: AWS Lambda is a serverless compute service where AWS manages the entire execution environment, including the OS and the language runtime. On EC2, the customer owns the OS and runtime. This is the key responsibility that shifts to AWS with Lambda.

choices.text: Writing the function code so that it validates and sanitizes all input parameters before processing.
choices.explanation: Input validation within application code is always the customer's responsibility, regardless of whether the code runs on Lambda or EC2. AWS does not author or validate customer application logic.

choices.text: Attaching an IAM execution role to the Lambda function with only the permissions it needs.
choices.explanation: IAM execution role configuration is a customer responsibility for Lambda functions. AWS does not attach or configure IAM roles on the customer's behalf.

choices.text: Encrypting environment variables that contain sensitive configuration values used by the function.
choices.explanation: Encrypting Lambda environment variables using AWS KMS is a customer configuration choice. AWS provides the capability, but enabling it remains the customer's decision.

questions.tip: Think about what a serverless model removes from the customer's operational scope compared to managing a virtual machine.
questions.explanation:
AWS Lambda is a fully managed serverless compute service. Unlike Amazon EC2, where customers are responsible for the guest OS and runtime environment, Lambda abstracts all of that away. AWS manages the OS, language runtime, security patches, and execution environment on behalf of the customer. The customer's responsibilities narrow to: function code, IAM execution roles, environment variable security, and VPC/network configuration if applicable.

**Why it works:** The OS and runtime layer is the clearest responsibility that migrates to AWS when moving from EC2 to Lambda.

**Why the others don't work:**
- Input validation in code: Application logic security is always the customer's responsibility.
- IAM execution role: Customers must still create and attach the correct role to their Lambda functions.
- Environment variable encryption: Enabling encryption for Lambda environment variables is a customer choice.

skills: 2.1.5: Describing how AWS responsibilities and customer responsibilities can shift, depending on the service used (for example, Amazon RDS, AWS Lambda, Amazon EC2).
questions.question: The following AWS compute and database services are listed in order from the service where the customer has the MOST security and operational responsibility to the service where the customer has the LEAST. Arrange them in that order.

choices.text: Amazon EC2 (customer manages OS, runtime, patching, and application stack).
choices.explanation: EC2 is IaaS. The customer is responsible for the full software stack above the hypervisor, giving them the highest level of responsibility of the three services.

choices.text: Amazon RDS (AWS manages OS and database engine; customer manages data, schema, and access).
choices.explanation: RDS is a managed database service. AWS absorbs the OS and engine layer, reducing customer responsibility compared to EC2, but the customer still manages data, access controls, and configuration choices.

choices.text: AWS Lambda (AWS manages OS, runtime, and execution environment; customer manages only function code and permissions).
choices.explanation: Lambda is serverless. AWS manages the complete execution environment, leaving the customer responsible only for function code, IAM execution roles, and application-level configuration. This is the lowest customer responsibility of the three.

questions.tip: Consider how much of the underlying software stack each service type requires the customer to manage directly.
questions.explanation: The shared responsibility model shifts as the level of abstraction increases. EC2 (IaaS) gives customers full control and full responsibility for the software stack. RDS (managed PaaS) moves OS and engine management to AWS, reducing customer scope. Lambda (serverless) goes furthest, with AWS owning the entire execution environment. The progression is: EC2 (most customer responsibility) to RDS (medium) to Lambda (least).

skills: 2.2.1: Identifying where to find AWS compliance information (for example, AWS Artifact).
questions.question:
During a security audit, the compliance officer at a healthcare organization needs to accept a Business Associate Addendum (BAA) with AWS to operate HIPAA-eligible workloads. The officer wants to complete this entirely through the AWS Management Console without involving AWS Support.

Which AWS service allows the organization to review and accept the BAA directly?

choices.text: AWS Artifact Agreements
choices.explanation: The Agreements section of AWS Artifact allows account administrators to review, accept, and manage agreements such as the Business Associate Addendum (BAA) directly from the AWS Management Console.

choices.text: AWS Organizations Service Control Policies
choices.explanation: AWS Organizations Service Control Policies (SCPs) control the maximum available permissions for accounts within an organization, but they are not the mechanism for accepting legal agreements such as the BAA.

choices.text: AWS IAM Identity Center
choices.explanation: AWS IAM Identity Center manages single sign-on access and permission sets across AWS accounts, but does not provide the ability to review or accept compliance agreements like the BAA.

choices.text: AWS Compliance Center
choices.explanation: The AWS Compliance Center is a publicly accessible research tool for understanding regulatory requirements by country or industry, but it does not allow customers to accept agreements with AWS.

questions.tip: Focus on the AWS service that handles both compliance documentation and the execution of customer agreements within the Management Console.
questions.explanation:
AWS Artifact Agreements is correct. Within AWS Artifact, the Agreements tab allows customers to accept legally binding agreements with AWS, including the Business Associate Addendum required for HIPAA-eligible workloads, all through the AWS Management Console.

**Why it works:** AWS Artifact was designed to centralize compliance documentation and agreement management, removing the need to contact AWS Support for common legal agreements.

**Why the others don't work:**
- AWS Organizations SCPs: These define permission boundaries for accounts and have no role in accepting legal agreements.
- AWS IAM Identity Center: Handles authentication and access federation, not compliance agreements.
- AWS Compliance Center: A public-facing informational tool that helps explore regulatory requirements, not a portal for executing agreements.

skills: 2.2.1: Identifying where to find AWS compliance information (for example, AWS Artifact).
questions.question: Match each compliance information need to the AWS resource that BEST fulfills it.

slots.label: Downloading a SOC 2 Type II report to provide to an external auditor
Accepting a Business Associate Addendum (BAA) to enable HIPAA-eligible workloads
Researching which AWS services are in scope for PCI DSS compliance

choices.text: AWS Artifact Reports
choices.explanation: The Reports section of AWS Artifact hosts downloadable compliance reports such as SOC 1, SOC 2, ISO 27001, and PCI DSS attestations.

choices.text: AWS Artifact Agreements
choices.explanation: The Agreements section of AWS Artifact is where customers review and accept legal agreements with AWS, including the HIPAA BAA.

choices.text: AWS Compliance Center or AWS documentation
choices.explanation: AWS publishes PCI DSS scope information and compliance program details through public documentation and the AWS Compliance Center, not as downloadable reports in Artifact.

questions.tip: Consider the two distinct sections within AWS Artifact and what each one is designed to provide.
questions.explanation: AWS Artifact has two primary functions: the Reports section provides downloadable third-party audit reports, and the Agreements section is used to review and accept legal agreements. Research about service-level compliance scope is covered by public AWS compliance documentation and the AWS Compliance Center.

skills: 2.2.2: Understanding compliance needs among geographic locations or industries (for example, AWS Compliance).
questions.question:
Following a board decision to expand operations into the European Union, a company's legal team must understand how AWS handles personal data of EU residents to satisfy General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR) requirements. They need documentation that AWS acts as a data processor and commits to appropriate safeguards.

Which AWS resource BEST addresses the legal team's need to establish a GDPR-compliant data processing relationship with AWS?

choices.text: The AWS Data Processing Addendum (DPA), accepted through AWS Artifact
choices.explanation: AWS provides a Data Processing Addendum that satisfies GDPR Article 28 requirements for controller-processor relationships. Customers accept this agreement through AWS Artifact.

choices.text: An AWS Support case requesting GDPR compliance confirmation, which generates a formal written response
choices.explanation: AWS Support cases handle technical and account issues. GDPR agreement execution is handled through self-service mechanisms in AWS Artifact, not through support tickets.

choices.text: An AWS Organizations policy that restricts all resource creation to the eu-west-1 Region, ensuring data residency
choices.explanation: Data residency controls can be implemented with AWS Organizations policies, but data residency alone does not satisfy the requirement for a formal data processing agreement between the customer and AWS as mandated by GDPR Article 28.

choices.text: An Amazon Macie scan of all S3 buckets in the account, which certifies that personal data is properly classified under GDPR
choices.explanation: Amazon Macie discovers and classifies sensitive data in Amazon S3, which supports GDPR data inventory efforts, but it does not establish a legal data processing relationship between the customer and AWS.

questions.tip: Consider what legal instrument is required between a data controller and a data processor under GDPR, and where AWS makes that instrument available.
questions.explanation:
The AWS Data Processing Addendum, accepted through AWS Artifact, is correct. GDPR Article 28 requires a written contract between a data controller and data processor. AWS's DPA fulfills this requirement and is accepted self-service through AWS Artifact.

**Why it works:** AWS Artifact serves as the central location where customers can accept formal legal agreements that govern how AWS processes customer data under various regulatory frameworks.

**Why the others don't work:**
- AWS Support case: Agreement execution is self-service in AWS Artifact; a support ticket is not the appropriate channel.
- AWS Organizations residency policy: Controls data location but does not constitute a data processing agreement.
- Amazon Macie scan: Assists with data classification and discovery, but produces findings rather than legal agreements.

skills: 2.2.2: Understanding compliance needs among geographic locations or industries (for example, AWS Compliance).
questions.question:
The operations team at a global retail company is assessing the AWS compliance programs relevant to their business. The company processes credit card payments and stores customer data in multiple countries, each with different regulatory requirements.

Which TWO statements accurately describe how AWS approaches compliance across different industries and geographies?

choices.text: AWS maintains compliance certifications and attestations for specific programs such as PCI DSS and ISO 27001, and publishes which services fall within the scope of each program
choices.explanation: AWS actively participates in compliance programs and publishes the list of services that are in scope for each certification, allowing customers to build compliant architectures using only eligible services.

choices.text: Compliance responsibility is shared: AWS is responsible for the compliance of the underlying cloud infrastructure, while customers are responsible for their applications, data, and configurations running on AWS
choices.explanation: Under the AWS shared responsibility model, AWS secures and certifies its global infrastructure, but customers must ensure their own workloads, data handling, and configurations meet applicable regulatory requirements.

choices.text: When a customer deploys a workload in an AWS Region, that workload automatically inherits all of the compliance certifications held by AWS for that Region, satisfying all local regulatory requirements
choices.explanation: Compliance certifications for AWS infrastructure do not automatically extend to customer workloads. Customers must implement their own controls and may need separate assessments to satisfy local regulatory requirements.

choices.text: AWS Regions in the European Union are certified under different compliance programs than all other Regions, so customers must deploy all regulated workloads exclusively in EU Regions
choices.explanation: While some compliance programs have geographic relevance (such as GDPR for EU data subjects), many certifications like ISO 27001 and PCI DSS apply to AWS infrastructure globally. Customers are not required to use only EU Regions to meet all regulatory obligations.

choices.text: By accepting a single AWS compliance agreement, a customer's workloads automatically become certified under all compliance programs that AWS participates in
choices.explanation: Each compliance program has its own requirements, agreements, and customer obligations. Accepting one agreement does not confer compliance across all programs; each must be addressed separately.

questions.tip: Consider how the shared responsibility model interacts with regulatory compliance, and what AWS actually certifies versus what customers must address independently.
questions.explanation:
AWS certifies its infrastructure under programs such as PCI DSS and ISO 27001 and publishes service scope lists, but customers retain responsibility for their own workloads and configurations under the shared responsibility model. These two facts together define how compliance works on AWS across industries and geographies.

**Why the others don't work:**
- Automatic inheritance: AWS certifications cover the infrastructure layer; customer workloads require their own controls and assessments.
- EU-only requirement: Many certifications apply globally, and geographic deployment decisions depend on specific regulatory requirements, not a blanket EU-only rule.
- Single agreement covering all programs: Each compliance program is distinct and must be addressed individually.

skills: 2.2.3: Describing how customers secure resources on AWS (for example, Amazon Inspector, AWS Security Hub, Amazon GuardDuty, AWS Shield).
questions.question:
You are a cloud security engineer responsible for ensuring that Amazon EC2 instances in your environment are free of known software vulnerabilities and do not have unintended ports exposed to the internet. Your team wants a service that automatically discovers instances, assesses them against a continuously updated CVE database, and produces prioritized findings.

Which AWS service is MOST suitable for performing automated vulnerability assessments of EC2 instances?

choices.text: Amazon Inspector
choices.explanation: Amazon Inspector automatically discovers EC2 instances and container images, scans them for software vulnerabilities using an up-to-date CVE database, and evaluates network reachability to flag unintended exposure, producing risk-scored findings.

choices.text: Amazon GuardDuty
choices.explanation: Amazon GuardDuty detects active threats and suspicious behavior by analyzing logs such as VPC Flow Logs and CloudTrail events. It does not perform software vulnerability assessments against a CVE database.

choices.text: AWS Security Hub
choices.explanation: AWS Security Hub aggregates findings from services like Amazon Inspector and Amazon GuardDuty and checks configurations against security standards. It does not independently scan instances for software vulnerabilities.

choices.text: AWS Systems Manager Patch Manager
choices.explanation: AWS Systems Manager Patch Manager automates the process of applying operating system and application patches to instances, but it does not assess instances against a CVE database to produce vulnerability findings.

questions.tip: Consider which service specifically performs vulnerability scanning against software packages and network reachability on EC2 instances.
questions.explanation:
Amazon Inspector is the correct choice. It automatically discovers EC2 instances and container images, continuously scans them for known vulnerabilities (CVEs), assesses network exposure, and provides risk-prioritized findings with remediation guidance.

**Why it works:** Inspector integrates with AWS Systems Manager Agent on EC2 instances to enumerate installed software packages and cross-reference them against the NVD and other CVE feeds.

**Why the others don't work:**
- Amazon GuardDuty: Detects threats from behavioral signals in log data, not software vulnerability scanning.
- AWS Security Hub: Aggregates and normalizes findings from multiple services but does not scan instances directly.
- AWS Systems Manager Patch Manager: Applies patches to remediate vulnerabilities but does not discover or assess vulnerabilities itself.

skills: 2.2.3: Describing how customers secure resources on AWS (for example, Amazon Inspector, AWS Security Hub, Amazon GuardDuty, AWS Shield).
questions.question: Arrange the following steps in the correct order to set up a centralized security monitoring posture for a new AWS account, starting from enabling individual detection services through to responding to aggregated findings.

choices.text: Enable Amazon GuardDuty to begin continuous threat detection by analyzing CloudTrail, VPC Flow Logs, and DNS logs
choices.explanation: GuardDuty should be enabled first as a foundational threat detection layer. It starts generating findings as soon as it is turned on with no additional configuration required.

choices.text: Enable Amazon Inspector to automatically discover EC2 instances and container images and assess them for software vulnerabilities
choices.explanation: Inspector can be enabled independently alongside GuardDuty to provide vulnerability assessment findings. Both services produce findings that can be centralized in Security Hub.

choices.text: Enable AWS Security Hub and configure it to ingest findings from GuardDuty and Inspector into a single consolidated view
choices.explanation: Security Hub is enabled after the detection services so it can aggregate and normalize their findings. Enabling it first without active sources produces no findings to consolidate.

choices.text: Review aggregated findings in AWS Security Hub and prioritize remediation based on severity scores
choices.explanation: After detection services are active and Security Hub is ingesting findings, security teams use the Security Hub console or API to triage and respond to prioritized findings.

questions.tip: Consider which services generate findings first and which service is used to aggregate those findings before any review can take place.
questions.explanation: The correct sequence starts with enabling GuardDuty and Inspector as detection sources, then enabling Security Hub to aggregate their output, and finally using Security Hub to review and prioritize remediation. Security Hub cannot provide value without active upstream detection services already generating findings.

skills: 2.2.4: Identifying different encryption options (for example, encryption in transit, encryption at rest).
questions.question:
Management has decided that all database connections from application servers to Amazon RDS instances must be secured so that sensitive data cannot be intercepted while moving across the network. The security team wants to enforce this without replacing the database engine.

Which encryption option should the team implement to protect data as it travels between the application servers and the Amazon RDS instances?

choices.text: Encryption in transit, by configuring the application to use SSL/TLS connections to Amazon RDS and enforcing encrypted connections with the `rds.force_ssl` parameter
choices.explanation: Encryption in transit using SSL/TLS protects data as it moves across the network between the application and the database. Amazon RDS supports TLS connections and provides an option to force all connections to use SSL via database parameters.

choices.text: Encryption at rest, by enabling Amazon RDS storage encryption with an AWS KMS key to prevent data from being read over the network
choices.explanation: Encryption at rest protects data stored on the RDS storage layer, not data traveling across the network. Enabling storage encryption does not prevent unencrypted network connections between the application and the database.

choices.text: Amazon VPC encryption, by placing both the application servers and the RDS instance in the same Availability Zone to encrypt all traffic between them
choices.explanation: Placing resources in the same Availability Zone reduces network latency but does not encrypt traffic. VPC networking within AWS does not encrypt traffic between instances by default; explicit TLS or other encryption must be applied.

choices.text: Encryption at rest, by enabling automatic backups on the Amazon RDS instance so that all data is stored in an encrypted snapshot
choices.explanation: Automatic backups create encrypted snapshots when storage encryption is enabled, but this protects data at rest in backups, not data transmitted over network connections between the application and the live database.

questions.tip: Focus on which encryption type covers data that is actively moving between two systems over a network connection.
questions.explanation:
Encryption in transit using SSL/TLS is correct. Configuring the application to initiate SSL/TLS connections and using the `rds.force_ssl` parameter to reject unencrypted connections ensures all data moving between the application servers and the RDS instances is protected.

**Why it works:** TLS encrypts the network channel, so even if traffic is intercepted, the data cannot be read without the session keys.

**Why the others don't work:**
- Encryption at rest with KMS: Protects stored data, not in-flight network traffic.
- Same Availability Zone placement: A network topology choice that reduces latency but provides no encryption.
- Encrypted backups: Protect stored backup data, not live network connections.

skills: 2.2.4: Identifying different encryption options (for example, encryption in transit, encryption at rest).
questions.question: Match each encryption scenario to the type of encryption it represents.

slots.label: An Amazon S3 object is encrypted with an AWS KMS key before being written to disk
An application uses HTTPS to send customer data to an Amazon API Gateway endpoint
An Amazon RDS instance stores its data volumes using AES-256 encryption managed by AWS KMS
An Amazon EC2 instance establishes a TLS connection to an external payment processing API

choices.text: Encryption at rest
choices.explanation: Encryption at rest protects data that is stored on a medium such as disk. S3 server-side encryption and RDS storage encryption both fall into this category.

choices.text: Encryption in transit
choices.explanation: Encryption in transit protects data as it moves across a network. HTTPS and TLS connections are the primary mechanisms for encryption in transit.

questions.tip: Ask whether the data is sitting in storage or actively moving between systems to determine which encryption type applies.
questions.explanation: Encryption at rest applies when data is protected while stored on a medium such as disk or object storage. Encryption in transit applies when data is protected while traveling across a network connection. S3 server-side encryption and RDS storage encryption are examples of at-rest encryption, while HTTPS and TLS connections are examples of in-transit encryption.

skills: 2.2.5: Recognizing services that aid in governance and compliance (for example, monitoring with Amazon CloudWatch; auditing with AWS CloudTrail, AWS Audit Manager, and AWS Config; reporting with access reports).
questions.question:
The engineering team is evaluating AWS services to help satisfy a regulatory requirement that all Amazon S3 buckets in the account must not allow public access. The team needs a service that continuously evaluates bucket configurations against this rule and automatically flags any bucket that becomes non-compliant over time.

Which AWS service is MOST appropriate for continuously evaluating whether resources comply with defined configuration rules?

choices.text: AWS Config
choices.explanation: AWS Config continuously evaluates resource configurations against managed or custom rules. It can detect when an Amazon S3 bucket's public access settings change to non-compliant and flag it, providing a compliance timeline and remediation options.

choices.text: AWS CloudTrail
choices.explanation: AWS CloudTrail records API calls and can show when a bucket policy was changed, but it does not evaluate resource configurations against a defined compliance rule or produce a pass/fail compliance status for each resource.

choices.text: Amazon CloudWatch alarms
choices.explanation: Amazon CloudWatch alarms trigger based on metric thresholds, such as CPU utilization or error rates. They do not evaluate resource configuration compliance against policy rules like S3 public access settings.

choices.text: AWS Audit Manager
choices.explanation: AWS Audit Manager automates the collection of evidence for audit frameworks and maps AWS usage to compliance controls. It builds on Config findings but does not itself perform continuous real-time rule evaluation against individual resource configurations.

questions.tip: Consider which service is specifically designed to evaluate whether AWS resource configurations match desired states on an ongoing basis.
questions.explanation:
AWS Config is correct. It continuously records resource configurations and evaluates them against rules - either AWS-managed rules or custom rules written with AWS Lambda. When an S3 bucket's public access configuration drifts from the desired state, Config flags it as non-compliant.

**Why it works:** Config provides a configuration history and a compliance timeline, making it possible to see not just current compliance status but also when a resource became non-compliant.

**Why the others don't work:**
- AWS CloudTrail: Records the history of API actions but does not evaluate configurations against rules or report compliance status.
- Amazon CloudWatch alarms: Monitor performance metrics and thresholds, not resource configuration state.
- AWS Audit Manager: Aggregates evidence for audits and frameworks, but relies on Config and other services for real-time configuration evaluation.

skills: 2.2.5: Recognizing services that aid in governance and compliance (for example, monitoring with Amazon CloudWatch; auditing with AWS CloudTrail, AWS Audit Manager, and AWS Config; reporting with access reports).
questions.question:
To reduce infrastructure costs, a company is consolidating its compliance tooling on AWS. The compliance manager needs to identify which services can provide direct evidence or records that can be used in a formal external audit to demonstrate governance and compliance over time.

Which TWO AWS services provide capabilities that directly support audit evidence collection and governance reporting?

choices.text: AWS CloudTrail, which records a history of API calls including caller identity, timestamp, and source IP, serving as an audit trail for all account activity
choices.explanation: CloudTrail provides an immutable record of all API activity in an AWS account, which is a primary source of audit evidence for demonstrating who performed what actions and when.

choices.text: AWS Audit Manager, which continuously collects evidence from AWS services and maps it to compliance frameworks such as PCI DSS, HIPAA, and SOC 2 to simplify audit preparation
choices.explanation: AWS Audit Manager automates evidence collection from services like CloudTrail, Config, and Security Hub, and organizes it against audit frameworks, directly reducing the manual effort required for formal audits.

choices.text: Amazon CloudWatch, which monitors application performance metrics and triggers alarms when thresholds are breached, providing a complete audit trail of all resource changes
choices.explanation: Amazon CloudWatch monitors operational metrics and logs but does not provide an audit trail of resource configuration changes or API call history. It complements governance tooling but is not a primary evidence source for compliance audits.

choices.text: AWS Systems Manager Session Manager, which records all terminal sessions to EC2 instances and automatically submits session logs as audit evidence to AWS Audit Manager
choices.explanation: AWS Systems Manager Session Manager can log session activity to Amazon S3 or CloudWatch Logs, but it does not automatically submit evidence to AWS Audit Manager. It addresses a narrow access-logging use case rather than broad governance reporting.

choices.text: Amazon EC2 Auto Scaling, which maintains records of scaling events and instance health checks that can be used as evidence of infrastructure availability in compliance reports
choices.explanation: EC2 Auto Scaling records scaling activities, but these are operational logs, not governance or compliance evidence. Auto Scaling is not designed as a compliance reporting or audit evidence tool.

questions.tip: Focus on services whose primary purpose includes recording account activity history or organizing that history against compliance frameworks.
questions.explanation:
AWS CloudTrail and AWS Audit Manager are the correct answers. CloudTrail creates an authoritative record of API activity that auditors rely on to verify account actions, while Audit Manager automates the collection and organization of evidence against formal compliance frameworks.

**Why the others don't work:**
- Amazon CloudWatch: An operational monitoring service that does not produce compliance audit evidence or resource change history.
- AWS Systems Manager Session Manager: Provides session logging for a specific access vector but does not integrate automatically with Audit Manager or produce broad compliance evidence.
- EC2 Auto Scaling: An operational service for managing compute capacity, not a compliance or governance reporting tool.

skills: 2.2.6: Recognizing compliance requirements that vary among AWS services.
questions.question:
The operations team at a payment processing company is designing a new application on AWS and must ensure all components used to store and process cardholder data are within scope for PCI DSS. The team is evaluating which AWS services to include in the architecture.

What should the team verify before finalizing the use of any AWS service in their PCI DSS-compliant architecture?

choices.text: Confirm that each service appears on the AWS PCI DSS Services in Scope list, since not all AWS services have been validated under the PCI DSS compliance program
choices.explanation: AWS publishes an official list of services that are in scope for each compliance program, including PCI DSS. Not all AWS services have been assessed, so only services on the in-scope list should be used for regulated workloads.

choices.text: Verify that all services are hosted in AWS Regions located in the same country as the cardholder data, since PCI DSS compliance only applies to same-country deployments
choices.explanation: PCI DSS is a global standard that applies regardless of geographic region. While data residency may be a separate business requirement, it is not the criterion that determines PCI DSS service eligibility on AWS.

choices.text: Confirm that each service has been enabled in the AWS Management Console, since only enabled services are covered under the AWS shared responsibility model
choices.explanation: All AWS services operate under the shared responsibility model once enabled, but whether a service is enabled does not determine its PCI DSS compliance scope. Scope is determined by whether AWS has had the service assessed by a Qualified Security Assessor.

choices.text: Ensure that all services are fully managed by AWS, since only fully managed services fall within PCI DSS scope and require no customer responsibility for compliance controls
choices.explanation: Whether a service is fully managed is not the criterion for PCI DSS scope. Some managed services are in scope and some are not. Even in-scope services still require customers to implement controls on their side of the shared responsibility model.

questions.tip: Consider that AWS publishes an authoritative, service-by-service list for each compliance program, and think about why not every AWS service appears on that list.
questions.explanation:
Confirming that each service is on the AWS PCI DSS Services in Scope list is correct. AWS undergoes annual PCI DSS assessments, but only specific services have been included in those assessments. Using a service not on the list would introduce an unvalidated component into the cardholder data environment.

**Why it works:** AWS explicitly documents which services have been assessed for each compliance program, allowing architects to make informed decisions about their regulated workloads.

**Why the others don't work:**
- Geographic region: PCI DSS is a global standard; compliance scope is not determined by deployment location.
- Enabled in console: Enabling a service has no bearing on its compliance program scope.
- Fully managed: Management model and PCI DSS scope are independent attributes of a service.

skills: 2.2.6: Recognizing compliance requirements that vary among AWS services.
questions.question: Arrange the following steps in the correct order for evaluating whether a specific AWS service can be used in a HIPAA-compliant workload, starting from the initial research phase through to ongoing monitoring.

choices.text: Consult the AWS HIPAA compliance page to determine whether the target service appears on the list of HIPAA-eligible services
choices.explanation: The first step is to verify eligibility. If the service is not on the HIPAA-eligible list, it cannot be used to process protected health information regardless of configuration.

choices.text: Accept the AWS Business Associate Addendum (BAA) through AWS Artifact to establish the required data processing agreement with AWS
choices.explanation: Before using any HIPAA-eligible service for protected health information, the customer must accept the BAA. Without it, using even an eligible service for PHI is not permitted under the AWS HIPAA compliance program.

choices.text: Implement the required customer-side controls for the service, such as encryption at rest, encryption in transit, and access logging, to satisfy HIPAA safeguards
choices.explanation: After confirming eligibility and accepting the BAA, the customer must configure the service according to HIPAA technical safeguards. These controls are the customer's responsibility under the shared responsibility model.

choices.text: Enable AWS Config rules to continuously monitor the service's configuration and alert on any drift from the required HIPAA-compliant state
choices.explanation: Ongoing monitoring with AWS Config ensures the service remains in a compliant configuration over time, detecting drift that could put the workload out of compliance.

questions.tip: Consider what must be confirmed and agreed upon before any configuration work begins, and what ongoing activity is required after the service is in use.
questions.explanation: The correct sequence is: verify HIPAA eligibility, accept the BAA, implement customer-side controls, and then establish ongoing configuration monitoring. Verifying eligibility must come first because implementing controls on an ineligible service does not make it HIPAA-compliant. The BAA must be in place before using the service for PHI. Customer controls must be applied before the workload goes live, and ongoing monitoring through AWS Config ensures sustained compliance.

skills: 2.3.1: Understanding access keys, password policies, and credential storage (for example, AWS Secrets Manager, AWS Systems Manager).
questions.question:
During a code review, a DevOps engineer discovers that database credentials are hardcoded directly in the application source code that is stored in a version control system. The engineering manager wants to remove all plaintext secrets from the codebase and ensure that the application retrieves credentials at runtime through a managed service that supports automatic rotation.

Which AWS service is MOST suitable for storing and automatically rotating these database credentials?

choices.text: AWS Secrets Manager
choices.explanation: AWS Secrets Manager is purpose-built for storing, managing, and automatically rotating secrets such as database credentials, API keys, and other sensitive configuration values.

choices.text: AWS Systems Manager Parameter Store
choices.explanation: Parameter Store can store secrets securely using SecureString parameters, but it does not natively provide automatic credential rotation. A separate Lambda function would need to be configured for rotation.

choices.text: AWS Key Management Service
choices.explanation: AWS KMS manages encryption keys used to protect data, but it does not store application secrets or rotate database credentials.

choices.text: Amazon S3 with server-side encryption
choices.explanation: Storing credentials in an encrypted S3 object does not provide secret management features such as access auditing, rotation policies, or SDK-native retrieval for application use.

questions.tip: Consider which service was specifically designed for secret lifecycle management, including built-in rotation support.
questions.explanation:
AWS Secrets Manager is designed to store sensitive credentials and provides native integration with Amazon RDS, Amazon Redshift, and other services to automatically rotate secrets on a configurable schedule without requiring application downtime.

**Why it works:** Secrets Manager handles the full lifecycle of a secret including creation, retrieval via SDK, rotation via Lambda, and auditing via AWS CloudTrail.

**Why the others don't work:**
- Parameter Store can store encrypted values but requires a custom Lambda function for rotation, making it less suitable when automatic rotation is a stated requirement.
- AWS KMS manages cryptographic keys, not application-level secrets or connection strings.
- Amazon S3 with encryption provides object storage, not a managed secret retrieval or rotation mechanism.

skills: 2.3.1: Understanding access keys, password policies, and credential storage (for example, AWS Secrets Manager, AWS Systems Manager).
questions.question: Match each credential management requirement to the AWS feature or service that directly addresses it.

slots.label: Enforce a minimum password length and require uppercase characters for IAM user console sign-ins
Store a third-party API key and automatically rotate it using a custom AWS Lambda function
Store a plaintext configuration value that does not require encryption or rotation
Identify which IAM users have access keys that have not been used in the past 180 days

choices.text: IAM account password policy
choices.explanation: The IAM account password policy controls console password requirements such as minimum length, complexity rules, and expiry periods.

choices.text: AWS Secrets Manager
choices.explanation: Secrets Manager supports storing arbitrary secrets and triggering automatic rotation via a Lambda function on a defined schedule.

choices.text: AWS Systems Manager Parameter Store (Standard tier)
choices.explanation: Parameter Store Standard tier is suited for storing non-sensitive configuration data that does not require encryption or rotation.

choices.text: IAM credential report
choices.explanation: The IAM credential report lists all users and includes access key last-used dates, making it the correct tool to identify stale credentials.

questions.tip: Think about the primary purpose of each AWS feature rather than its secondary capabilities.
questions.explanation: Each AWS feature has a distinct primary role in credential management. The IAM account password policy governs IAM user console passwords. AWS Secrets Manager manages the full lifecycle of secrets including automatic rotation. AWS Systems Manager Parameter Store stores configuration values at varying levels of sensitivity. IAM credential reports provide a snapshot of credential usage across all IAM users.

skills: 2.3.2: Identifying authentication methods in AWS (for example, multi-factor authentication [MFA], IAM Identity Center, cross-account IAM roles).
questions.question:
The operations team manages resources in three separate AWS accounts: a development account, a staging account, and a production account. Developers have IAM users in the development account and regularly need to access Amazon EC2 instances in the production account for read-only troubleshooting. The security team wants to avoid creating duplicate IAM users in the production account.

What is the MOST secure way to grant the developers access to the production account without creating additional IAM users there?

choices.text: Create a cross-account IAM role in the production account with the required read-only permissions, and grant the developers' IAM users in the development account permission to assume that role.
choices.explanation: Cross-account IAM roles allow users in one AWS account to assume a role in another account, providing temporary credentials scoped to the defined permissions without requiring duplicate IAM users.

choices.text: Share the root user credentials for the production account with the developers so they can sign in directly when troubleshooting is needed.
choices.explanation: Sharing root user credentials is a critical security violation. Root credentials should never be shared, and root access should be locked down with MFA and used only for account-level tasks.

choices.text: Create read-only IAM users in the production account for each developer and distribute the access keys to the developers in the development account.
choices.explanation: Creating duplicate IAM users in the production account is exactly what the security team wants to avoid. It also results in long-lived credentials being distributed, increasing risk.

choices.text: Attach a resource-based policy to the Amazon EC2 instances in the production account that allows the developers' IAM user ARNs to perform read-only API calls directly.
choices.explanation: Amazon EC2 instances do not support resource-based policies that grant cross-account access to EC2 API actions. Cross-account access to EC2 is achieved through IAM roles, not instance-level resource policies.

questions.tip: Think about the AWS mechanism that provides temporary, scoped credentials across account boundaries without duplicating identities.
questions.explanation:
Cross-account IAM roles are the standard AWS pattern for granting users in one account access to resources in another. The role is created in the target (production) account with a trust policy identifying the source account or specific IAM users. Developers in the development account then call `sts:AssumeRole` to obtain temporary credentials scoped to the role's permissions.

**Why it works:** Temporary credentials from role assumption expire automatically, reducing exposure. No long-lived credentials are created in the production account.

**Why the others don't work:**
- Sharing root credentials is a security anti-pattern and violates AWS best practices.
- Duplicate IAM users in the production account is the exact problem the team is trying to avoid.
- EC2 instances do not support resource-based policies for API-level cross-account access.

skills: 2.3.2: Identifying authentication methods in AWS (for example, multi-factor authentication [MFA], IAM Identity Center, cross-account IAM roles).
questions.question:
The engineering team is evaluating authentication options for a company that is moving to AWS and wants a centralised way to manage employee access to multiple AWS accounts using their existing corporate directory. The company also wants employees to authenticate with MFA and have a single sign-on portal.

Which TWO capabilities does AWS IAM Identity Center provide that directly support these requirements?

choices.text: Integration with an external identity provider or Microsoft Active Directory so that employees can authenticate using their existing corporate credentials.
choices.explanation: IAM Identity Center supports connecting to external identity providers via SAML 2.0 and to AWS Managed Microsoft AD or AD Connector, enabling employees to log in with corporate credentials.

choices.text: A built-in MFA capability that can be enforced for all users signing in through the IAM Identity Center portal, satisfying the MFA requirement without separate per-account configuration.
choices.explanation: IAM Identity Center provides centralized MFA enforcement at the portal level, so administrators can require MFA for all users from a single configuration, rather than configuring MFA separately in each AWS account.

choices.text: Automatic generation and rotation of long-term IAM access keys for each employee so that they can access multiple AWS accounts programmatically without signing into the portal.
choices.explanation: IAM Identity Center issues temporary credentials for CLI and SDK access, not long-term access keys. Automatically generating and rotating long-term keys for employees is not a feature of IAM Identity Center.

choices.text: A dedicated per-account MFA device registry where each employee must register a separate physical MFA token for every AWS account they are granted access to.
choices.explanation: IAM Identity Center provides a single centralised MFA configuration for the portal. Employees do not need to register separate MFA devices per account; the MFA is authenticated once at the portal level.

choices.text: Replacement of all AWS account root users with federated identities so that no root credentials exist in any account once IAM Identity Center is enabled.
choices.explanation: IAM Identity Center does not eliminate or replace root users. Each AWS account always has a root user with its own credentials. IAM Identity Center manages access through permission sets and federated sign-in, not root user replacement.

questions.tip: Focus on what IAM Identity Center centralises across accounts versus what remains per-account or per-user.
questions.explanation:
AWS IAM Identity Center (formerly AWS SSO) provides a centralised portal for access management across multiple AWS accounts. It integrates with external identity providers and corporate directories for federated authentication, and it offers centralized MFA enforcement so employees authenticate once with a second factor to access all their permitted accounts.

**Why the others don't work:**
- IAM Identity Center issues short-term credentials for CLI use, not long-term access keys.
- MFA in Identity Center is managed centrally at the portal level, not as separate per-account device registries.
- Root users always exist in AWS accounts and cannot be replaced by IAM Identity Center federated identities.

skills: 2.3.3: Defining groups, users, custom policies, and managed policies in compliance with the principle of least privilege.
questions.question:
The security compliance team at a healthcare company needs to create a permission set that grants a billing team access to AWS Cost Explorer and AWS Budgets but explicitly denies access to all Amazon EC2 and Amazon RDS resources. This permission set will need to be reused across multiple IAM groups and roles throughout the organisation.

Which type of IAM policy is BEST suited for this use case?

choices.text: An AWS managed policy chosen from the list of AWS-provided policies that most closely matches the required permissions.
choices.explanation: AWS managed policies are maintained by AWS and reflect general use cases. They cannot be customised to include an explicit Deny on specific services, making them unsuitable when a tailored permission boundary is required.

choices.text: A customer managed policy that defines exactly the required Allow and Deny statements, stored in IAM for reuse across multiple groups and roles.
choices.explanation: Customer managed policies are reusable, versioned IAM policies created by the account owner. They can contain precisely crafted Allow and Deny statements and can be attached to multiple principals, making them ideal for this scenario.

choices.text: An inline policy embedded directly in each IAM group that needs the permissions, with identical policy documents copied into each group.
choices.explanation: Inline policies are embedded in a single principal and cannot be shared. Copying identical inline policies into multiple groups creates redundancy and makes updates error-prone, violating the reuse requirement.

choices.text: A service control policy applied at the AWS Organizations root level that grants billing access and denies EC2 and RDS access across all accounts in the organisation.
choices.explanation: Service control policies operate at the AWS Organizations level and set maximum permissions for accounts, not for individual IAM groups or roles within an account. Using an SCP at the root level would affect all users in all accounts, which is broader than the stated requirement.

questions.tip: Focus on which policy type supports reuse across multiple IAM entities and allows the author to define custom Allow and Deny logic.
questions.explanation:
Customer managed policies are IAM policies created and owned by the account administrator. They can be attached to multiple IAM users, groups, and roles, and they support full policy language including explicit Deny statements. This makes them the correct choice when a specific, reusable permission set is needed across the organisation.

**Why it works:** Customer managed policies are versioned, can be audited, and can be attached to any number of principals simultaneously.

**Why the others don't work:**
- AWS managed policies cannot be customised; they reflect generic use cases maintained by AWS.
- Inline policies are bound to a single principal and cannot be reused.
- SCPs operate at the organisation or account level and are not scoped to individual IAM groups or roles within an account.

skills: 2.3.3: Defining groups, users, custom policies, and managed policies in compliance with the principle of least privilege.
questions.question: A cloud administrator needs to set up a new developer so they have only the permissions required for their role. Arrange the following IAM setup steps in the correct order to follow the principle of least privilege.

choices.text: Identify the specific AWS services and actions the developer needs to perform their job.
choices.explanation: Determining the required permissions first ensures the policy is based on actual need rather than convenience, which is the foundation of least privilege.

choices.text: Create a customer managed IAM policy that grants only the identified actions on the relevant resources.
choices.explanation: Once requirements are known, a policy is written that grants exactly those permissions - no more, no less.

choices.text: Create an IAM group that represents the developer's role, then attach the customer managed policy to the group.
choices.explanation: Attaching the policy to a group rather than directly to a user enables reuse and easier management when the team grows or roles change.

choices.text: Create an IAM user for the developer and add them to the group.
choices.explanation: The user inherits the group's permissions upon being added, following the established least-privilege policy without requiring direct policy attachment to the user.

choices.text: Review the developer's actual access patterns after a period of use and adjust the policy to remove any permissions that were not exercised.
choices.explanation: IAM Access Analyzer and credential reports can reveal unused permissions. Removing them after a review period tightens the least-privilege posture over time.

questions.tip: Consider which steps must be complete before subsequent ones can be done correctly - you cannot create a policy before knowing what it should allow.
questions.explanation: Following the principle of least privilege requires first understanding what access is truly needed, then building the policy to match, then structuring groups and users to inherit that policy cleanly. A final review step closes the loop by removing permissions that were granted but never used.

skills: 2.3.4: Identifying tasks that only the account root user can perform.
questions.question:
Management has decided to restructure AWS billing so that invoices are sent to a new corporate email address and a different credit card is on file. The current billing contact email and payment method need to be updated in the AWS account settings. The finance team's IAM administrator attempts the change but cannot find the option.

Which statement best explains this situation?

choices.text: Updating the account's primary contact email address and the default payment method are root user tasks that cannot be delegated to IAM users through permissions.
choices.explanation: Changing the account root email address and updating the primary payment method are among the tasks reserved exclusively for the root user. No IAM policy grants these capabilities to other principals.

choices.text: The IAM administrator needs to be granted the `aws-portal:ModifyBilling` permission in their IAM policy, after which they can update the payment method and email address.
choices.explanation: While some billing console access can be granted via IAM, updating the root account email address is not a delegatable action. Additionally, `aws-portal:ModifyBilling` does not cover root account contact changes.

choices.text: Changes to billing contact information require a support ticket submitted to AWS Billing Support, which then updates the account settings on behalf of the user.
choices.explanation: AWS does not require a support ticket to update billing contact information or payment methods. These changes are made directly in the AWS Management Console by the root user.

choices.text: The IAM administrator must first enable IAM access to billing information in the account settings, after which they will be able to update all account-level billing fields including the primary contact email.
choices.explanation: Enabling IAM access to billing allows IAM users to view and manage some billing information such as Cost Explorer and invoices, but it does not grant the ability to change the account root email address or primary payment method, which remain root-only tasks.

questions.tip: Think about which account-level fields are tied directly to the root user identity rather than to billing permissions.
questions.explanation:
AWS accounts have a small number of operations that are permanently reserved for the root user. Changing the account email address (which is the root user's sign-in identifier) and updating the default payment method fall into this category. These are not accessible via IAM policies or billing console access grants.

**Why it works:** The root user owns the account identity and financial information. These settings are tied to root account ownership, not to delegated permissions.

**Why the others don't work:**
- IAM billing permissions grant access to billing dashboards and reports, not to root identity fields such as the sign-in email.
- AWS Support is not the mechanism for updating account contact or payment details.
- Enabling IAM billing access expands billing visibility for IAM users but does not include root-only account identity changes.

skills: 2.3.4: Identifying tasks that only the account root user can perform.
questions.question: For each AWS account task, identify whether it is restricted to the root user only or whether it can be performed by an IAM user with sufficient permissions.

slots.label: Closing the AWS account
Creating an IAM user
Changing the AWS account root email address
Viewing AWS CloudTrail event history
Activating IAM access to the AWS Billing and Cost Management console

choices.text: Root user only - cannot be delegated to an IAM user
choices.explanation: These tasks are permanently reserved for the account root user regardless of IAM permissions.

choices.text: Can be performed by an IAM user with the appropriate permissions
choices.explanation: These tasks can be granted to IAM users through policies and are routinely performed by administrators without root access.

questions.tip: Root-only tasks are typically those that affect the account identity itself or have irreversible account-level consequences.
questions.explanation: AWS reserves a specific set of tasks for the account root user that cannot be performed by any IAM principal regardless of their attached policies. These include closing the account, changing the root sign-in email, and enabling IAM access to billing. Routine administration tasks such as creating IAM users and viewing CloudTrail logs can be fully delegated to IAM users with the correct permissions.

skills: 2.3.5: Understanding which methods can achieve root user protection.
questions.question:
After reviewing quarterly spending, a security team discovers that the AWS account root user has been signing in regularly to perform tasks that could be handled by IAM users. The team wants to harden the root user account to protect it from unauthorised access and ensure it is only used when absolutely necessary.

Which TWO actions should the team take to protect the root user?

choices.text: Enable multi-factor authentication on the root user account so that a second factor is required whenever the root user signs in.
choices.explanation: Enabling MFA on the root user is one of the highest-priority security recommendations from AWS. It ensures that even if the root password is compromised, an attacker cannot sign in without the second factor.

choices.text: Delete the root user access keys if they exist, so that the root user cannot be used for programmatic API access.
choices.explanation: Root user access keys provide programmatic access with unrestricted permissions. AWS recommends deleting these keys so that root cannot be invoked via the API, reducing the risk of automated exploitation.

choices.text: Attach an IAM policy to the root user that denies all actions except those reserved for root, limiting what the root user can do in the account.
choices.explanation: IAM policies cannot be attached to the root user. The root user's permissions are not governed by IAM policies; it always has full access to the account.

choices.text: Create a Service Control Policy in AWS Organizations that restricts the root user to specific AWS Regions, preventing global root user access.
choices.explanation: While SCPs can restrict member account root users in some scenarios when AWS Organizations is used, they do not restrict the root user of the management account. Additionally, the scenario does not mention Organizations, and this is not one of the primary root protection methods.

choices.text: Convert the root user into a standard IAM user by changing its IAM user type in the account settings, so that normal IAM policies can govern its access.
choices.explanation: The root user cannot be converted into an IAM user. These are fundamentally different account constructs; the root user identity is permanent and separate from IAM users.

questions.tip: Consider the two fundamental controls AWS recommends for securing any highly privileged account identity.
questions.explanation:
The two primary methods for protecting the AWS root user are enabling MFA and deleting root user access keys. MFA ensures that interactive sign-in requires more than just a password, while removing access keys prevents any programmatic use of root credentials.

**Why the others don't work:**
- IAM policies cannot be attached to the root user; root always has unrestricted access.
- SCPs have limited and complex applicability to the root user and are not the primary protection mechanism.
- The root user cannot be converted to a standard IAM user; they are different identity types.

skills: 2.3.5: Understanding which methods can achieve root user protection.
questions.question: A newly created AWS account needs to be secured before the team begins deploying workloads. Arrange the following root user protection steps in the recommended order.

choices.text: Sign in as the root user and check whether root user access keys exist in the Security Credentials section.
