choices.text: AWS Global Accelerator, which routes UDP and TCP traffic over the AWS global network using static anycast IP addresses, providing consistent low-latency performance for non-HTTP workloads.
choices.explanation: AWS Global Accelerator supports TCP and UDP protocols, provides two static anycast IP addresses that do not change, and routes traffic over the AWS global backbone to the nearest healthy endpoint. These characteristics make it well-suited for latency-sensitive non-HTTP applications such as gaming.

choices.text: Amazon CloudFront, which distributes UDP game traffic to edge locations worldwide and provides static IP addresses per distribution for use in customer firewall configurations.
choices.explanation: Amazon CloudFront is designed for HTTP/HTTPS workloads and caches content. It does not support UDP traffic and does not provide static anycast IP addresses for a distribution.

choices.text: Amazon Route 53 with latency-based routing, configured with health checks to route UDP traffic to the AWS Region with the lowest measured latency for each player.
choices.explanation: Route 53 latency-based routing resolves DNS queries to lower-latency endpoints, but DNS-level routing introduces variability due to DNS caching and TTLs. It does not provide static anycast IPs and does not optimize the network path at the packet level the way Global Accelerator does.

choices.text: AWS Direct Connect, configured with a dedicated connection from AWS to a network exchange point on each continent to provide low-latency access for players near those exchange points.
choices.explanation: AWS Direct Connect provides private, dedicated connectivity between on-premises locations and AWS for enterprise use cases. It is not a consumer-facing edge service and cannot be deployed for individual gaming players.

questions.tip: Consider which edge service supports non-HTTP protocols and provides fixed IP addresses that can be whitelisted at client firewalls.
questions.explanation:
AWS Global Accelerator is designed for applications that require consistent, low-latency performance for TCP and UDP workloads. It provides two static anycast IP addresses, routes traffic over the AWS global backbone, and supports non-HTTP protocols, making it the right choice for real-time gaming.

**Why it works:** Global Accelerator supports UDP, uses the AWS global backbone to reduce latency, and provides static anycast IPs that simplify firewall configuration.

**Why the others don't work:**
- Amazon CloudFront: HTTP/HTTPS CDN only; no UDP support and no static IPs per distribution.
- Route 53 latency-based routing: DNS-level only, subject to caching delays, no packet-level routing optimization.
- AWS Direct Connect: enterprise private connectivity, not a consumer-facing edge deployment model.

skills: 3.5.4: Identifying edge services (for example, CloudFront, Global Accelerator).
questions.question: Match each use case to the AWS edge service that BEST addresses it.

slots.label: Caching and delivering static images and videos to a global web audience with reduced origin load
Routing TCP and UDP application traffic over the AWS global backbone with static anycast IP addresses
Running serverless code at AWS edge locations to customize HTTP request and response handling
Providing instant failover between AWS Regions for a non-HTTP application with consistent performance requirements

choices.text: Amazon CloudFront as a content delivery network
choices.explanation: CloudFront caches content at edge locations to reduce latency and origin load for web and media delivery.

choices.text: AWS Global Accelerator for TCP/UDP routing with static IPs
choices.explanation: Global Accelerator routes TCP and UDP traffic over the AWS backbone using static anycast IPs, suitable for non-HTTP workloads.

choices.text: Amazon CloudFront with CloudFront Functions or Lambda@Edge
choices.explanation: CloudFront Functions and Lambda@Edge allow serverless code to run at CloudFront edge locations to customize HTTP behavior.

choices.text: AWS Global Accelerator for multi-Region failover
choices.explanation: Global Accelerator continuously monitors endpoint health and reroutes traffic to healthy endpoints in other Regions within seconds, supporting non-HTTP failover.

questions.tip: Consider whether each scenario requires content caching, protocol-level routing, code execution, or availability failover at the edge.
questions.explanation: Amazon CloudFront is optimized for HTTP/HTTPS content delivery and caching, and it integrates with Lambda@Edge and CloudFront Functions for edge compute. AWS Global Accelerator is optimized for consistent low-latency routing of TCP and UDP traffic using the AWS global backbone, with built-in health checking and multi-Region failover.

skills: 3.5.5: Identifying network connectivity options to AWS (for example, AWS VPN, Direct Connect).
questions.question:
After reviewing quarterly spending, the financial services company has identified that large-scale data transfer between their on-premises data warehouse and Amazon S3 is generating significant internet egress costs. The workload transfers several terabytes daily and requires consistent, predictable throughput. The company is willing to make a longer-term infrastructure investment to address this.

Which connectivity option provides the MOST cost-effective and consistent network performance for this workload?

choices.text: AWS Direct Connect, which provides a dedicated private connection with consistent throughput and reduced data transfer rates compared to internet-based transfer.
choices.explanation: AWS Direct Connect establishes a dedicated physical network connection between on-premises infrastructure and AWS. It offers consistent, high-throughput performance without internet variability, and data transferred over Direct Connect typically has lower per-GB pricing than standard internet egress rates.

choices.text: AWS Site-to-Site VPN, which routes data over the public internet using IPsec tunnels and reduces egress costs by compressing traffic before sending it to Amazon S3.
choices.explanation: AWS Site-to-Site VPN routes traffic over the public internet and does not offer reduced data transfer pricing or compression. Internet egress costs and bandwidth variability would persist, making it unsuitable for consistent high-volume transfers.

choices.text: Amazon S3 Transfer Acceleration, which routes uploads through AWS edge locations to maximize transfer speed over the public internet and reduces data transfer costs for large workloads.
choices.explanation: Amazon S3 Transfer Acceleration uses CloudFront edge locations to speed up uploads over the internet. It adds per-GB cost to transfers and does not reduce egress fees. It does not replace a dedicated connection for consistent high-volume workloads.

choices.text: AWS PrivateLink, which enables private connectivity from the on-premises data warehouse to Amazon S3 over the AWS network without requiring a dedicated physical connection or internet routing.
choices.explanation: AWS PrivateLink provides private connectivity between VPCs and AWS services without traversing the public internet, but it operates within the AWS network and requires existing connectivity (such as Direct Connect or VPN) to reach AWS from on-premises. It does not itself provide the underlying physical or VPN link.

questions.tip: Consider which connectivity option is designed for predictable, high-throughput workloads and offers reduced data transfer pricing compared to standard internet egress.
questions.explanation:
AWS Direct Connect provides a dedicated, private network connection to AWS that bypasses the public internet. It offers consistent throughput for large-scale data transfer workloads and typically results in lower per-GB data transfer costs compared to internet-based transfers.

**Why it works:** Direct Connect avoids internet egress fees and variability, providing predictable high-bandwidth performance suitable for multi-terabyte daily transfers.

**Why the others don't work:**
- AWS Site-to-Site VPN: uses the internet and does not reduce egress pricing.
- S3 Transfer Acceleration: adds cost and does not reduce egress fees for the volumes described.
- AWS PrivateLink: requires an existing underlying connection to AWS from on-premises and is not itself a connectivity service.

skills: 3.5.5: Identifying network connectivity options to AWS (for example, AWS VPN, Direct Connect).
questions.question:
The organization is looking to establish reliable connectivity between multiple on-premises offices and their AWS environment. The team is reviewing the characteristics of AWS connectivity options to determine which best fits each branch's requirements. Some branches need fast setup, while others require dedicated bandwidth.

Which TWO statements accurately describe AWS network connectivity options?

choices.text: AWS Site-to-Site VPN can be provisioned quickly over an existing internet connection and uses IPsec to encrypt traffic between the customer gateway and the virtual private gateway.
choices.explanation: Site-to-Site VPN requires only an internet connection and a compatible customer gateway device. It uses IPsec encryption and can typically be configured within hours.

choices.text: AWS Direct Connect provides a dedicated private network connection to AWS that does not traverse the public internet, offering consistent throughput and potentially lower data transfer costs for high-volume workloads.
choices.explanation: Direct Connect bypasses the public internet entirely, providing consistent latency and throughput. It typically offers lower per-GB pricing than internet egress for high-volume data transfer scenarios.

choices.text: AWS Direct Connect automatically encrypts all data in transit using AES-256 encryption by default, providing security without requiring additional configuration.
choices.explanation: AWS Direct Connect does not encrypt traffic by default. Organizations requiring encryption over Direct Connect must implement it separately, for example by running a Site-to-Site VPN over a Direct Connect public virtual interface or using MACsec on supported connections.

choices.text: AWS Site-to-Site VPN guarantees dedicated bandwidth between the on-premises location and AWS, unaffected by other internet traffic on the customer's connection.
choices.explanation: Site-to-Site VPN routes traffic over the public internet, so bandwidth is shared and subject to internet variability. It does not provide dedicated or guaranteed bandwidth. Dedicated bandwidth is a feature of AWS Direct Connect.

choices.text: Amazon VPC peering can be used to connect an on-premises data center to an Amazon VPC, providing encrypted connectivity similar to a VPN tunnel without requiring a customer gateway device.
choices.explanation: VPC peering connects two Amazon VPCs within or across AWS accounts and Regions. It cannot connect on-premises environments to AWS. On-premises connectivity requires Site-to-Site VPN or Direct Connect.

questions.tip: Focus on the fundamental characteristics of each connectivity type, particularly around encryption defaults, setup time, and bandwidth guarantees.
questions.explanation:
AWS provides two primary options for on-premises to AWS connectivity. Site-to-Site VPN is quick to set up over internet infrastructure and includes IPsec encryption. Direct Connect offers a private, consistent-bandwidth connection with potentially lower data transfer costs but requires physical circuit provisioning.

**Why they work:** Site-to-Site VPN's IPsec encryption and quick provisioning are accurate defining characteristics. Direct Connect's private path and consistent throughput are its primary differentiators.

**Why the others don't work:**
- Direct Connect default encryption: Direct Connect does not encrypt by default; encryption is an add-on.
- Site-to-Site VPN dedicated bandwidth: VPN traffic shares public internet capacity with no dedicated guarantee.
- VPC peering for on-premises: VPC peering only connects VPCs to each other, not on-premises locations to AWS.

skills: 3.6.1: Identifying the uses for object storage.
questions.question:
You are designing a backup solution for a company that generates thousands of log files, images, and PDF reports each day. The solution must retain files durably for several years, allow retrieval by a unique identifier, and require minimal management overhead.

Which storage model does Amazon S3 implement?

choices.text: Object storage, where each item is stored as a discrete object with a unique key, metadata, and the data itself.
choices.explanation: S3 is an object store. Every item is stored as a flat object with a key, metadata, and data payload rather than as a block or file-system entry.

choices.text: Block storage, where data is divided into fixed-size chunks and addressed by block offsets within a volume.
choices.explanation: Block storage (as used by Amazon EBS) addresses data at the block level within a volume. S3 does not use this model.

choices.text: File storage, where data is organized in a hierarchical directory tree and accessed with file-system operations.
choices.explanation: File storage (as used by Amazon EFS or Amazon FSx) organises data in directories. S3 uses a flat namespace with key prefixes that simulate a hierarchy but is not a true file system.

choices.text: Tape storage, where data is written sequentially and retrieved by rewinding to specific tape positions.
choices.explanation: Tape storage is sequential-access media. S3 provides random, key-based access to any object at any time without sequential retrieval.

questions.tip: Think about how data is uniquely addressed and what metadata accompanies each stored item.
questions.explanation:
Amazon S3 is an object storage service. Data is stored as self-contained objects, each with a unique key, optional user-defined metadata, and the data payload. This flat storage model differs fundamentally from block storage (which addresses raw sectors) and file storage (which uses directory hierarchies).

**Why it works:** Object storage stores items individually with rich metadata and unique keys, which matches the retrieval-by-identifier requirement at scale.

**Why the others don't work:**
- Block storage: raw sector-level addressing used by EBS volumes on EC2 instances.
- File storage: hierarchical directory model used by EFS and FSx.
- Tape storage: sequential access media; S3 is a random-access service.

skills: 3.6.1: Identifying the uses for object storage.
questions.question: Match each storage characteristic to the AWS storage model it describes.

slots.label: Data is stored as discrete items, each addressed by a unique key and accompanied by metadata.
Data is divided into fixed-size chunks and written to a volume addressable at the block level.
Data is organized in a directory hierarchy and accessed using standard file-system operations.

choices.text: Object storage (Amazon S3)
choices.explanation: S3 stores data as objects with unique keys and metadata, fitting the object storage model.

choices.text: Block storage (Amazon EBS)
choices.explanation: EBS presents raw block volumes to EC2 instances, matching the block-level addressing description.

choices.text: File storage (Amazon EFS)
choices.explanation: EFS provides a POSIX-compatible file system with directory hierarchies, matching the file-system operations description.

questions.tip: Consider how each model uniquely addresses stored data and what interface it exposes to applications.
questions.explanation: AWS offers three primary storage models. Object storage (Amazon S3) stores each item as an object with a unique key and metadata. Block storage (Amazon EBS) presents volumes as raw blocks to EC2 instances. File storage (Amazon EFS) provides a hierarchical file system accessed via NFS.

skills: 3.6.2: Recognizing the differences in Amazon S3 storage classes.
questions.question:
The operations team stores financial audit reports in Amazon S3. The reports are accessed frequently during the first 30 days after creation, then rarely queried for the following year before being permanently deleted. The team wants to reduce storage costs without changing the bucket configuration each month.

Which Amazon S3 storage class BEST automates tiering for this access pattern?

choices.text: S3 Intelligent-Tiering, which automatically moves objects between frequent-access and infrequent-access tiers based on observed access patterns.
choices.explanation: S3 Intelligent-Tiering monitors access patterns and automatically moves objects between tiers, eliminating the need for manual reconfiguration and optimising cost as access frequency changes.

choices.text: S3 Standard, which provides high durability and millisecond latency but applies a flat storage price regardless of how often objects are accessed.
choices.explanation: S3 Standard does not tier data based on access frequency, so infrequently accessed objects continue to incur Standard pricing rather than a lower tier.

choices.text: S3 Glacier Instant Retrieval, which stores archival data at low cost and retrieves objects in milliseconds but is designed for data accessed only once a quarter.
choices.explanation: Glacier Instant Retrieval is optimised for quarterly or less frequent access and carries retrieval costs; it is not designed for the automatic tiering needed in this scenario.

choices.text: S3 One Zone-IA, which reduces cost by storing objects in a single Availability Zone and is suited for infrequently accessed data that can be recreated if lost.
choices.explanation: S3 One Zone-IA stores data in a single AZ, reducing durability. It does not automatically adjust its tier based on changing access patterns.

questions.tip: Look for the storage class that adapts to changing access patterns automatically rather than requiring manual lifecycle rule updates.
questions.explanation:
S3 Intelligent-Tiering is designed for data with unpredictable or evolving access patterns. It monitors each object's access history and automatically moves objects to the most cost-effective tier without operational overhead or retrieval fees for objects moved to the infrequent-access tier.

**Why it works:** Intelligent-Tiering removes the need for manual lifecycle rules by automatically shifting objects as access frequency changes.

**Why the others don't work:**
- S3 Standard: flat pricing regardless of access frequency; no automatic tiering.
- S3 Glacier Instant Retrieval: archival tier designed for quarterly access; incurs retrieval fees and is not auto-tiering.
- S3 One Zone-IA: single-AZ storage for infrequent access; does not adapt to changing access patterns.

skills: 3.6.2: Recognizing the differences in Amazon S3 storage classes.
questions.question:
After reviewing quarterly spending, a data engineering team identifies that 80 percent of objects in their Amazon S3 bucket are compliance archives that have not been accessed in over two years. The team needs the LOWEST possible storage cost for these objects and can accept retrieval times of several hours.

Which S3 storage class meets this requirement?

choices.text: S3 Glacier Deep Archive, which offers the lowest storage cost in Amazon S3 and is designed for long-term retention with retrieval times of 12 hours or more.
choices.explanation: S3 Glacier Deep Archive is the lowest-cost S3 storage class, intended for data retained for 7 to 10 years or longer where retrieval within hours is acceptable.

choices.text: S3 Standard-IA, which reduces storage cost compared to S3 Standard and provides millisecond retrieval but charges a per-GB retrieval fee on each access.
choices.explanation: S3 Standard-IA offers lower storage costs than S3 Standard but is significantly more expensive than Glacier Deep Archive and provides faster retrieval than required.

choices.text: S3 Glacier Flexible Retrieval, which provides low-cost archival storage and supports retrieval options ranging from minutes to hours at a higher storage price than Deep Archive.
choices.explanation: Glacier Flexible Retrieval is cheaper than S3 Standard-IA but more expensive than Glacier Deep Archive. Deep Archive is the correct choice when the absolute lowest cost is required and multi-hour retrieval is acceptable.

choices.text: S3 Intelligent-Tiering, which monitors access patterns and moves infrequently accessed objects to an archive tier, but incurs a monthly monitoring fee per object.
choices.explanation: S3 Intelligent-Tiering charges a per-object monitoring fee and does not offer storage costs as low as Glacier Deep Archive for objects that are definitively never accessed.

questions.tip: Focus on which storage class is positioned as the absolute lowest cost tier and is specifically designed for data accessed very rarely.
questions.explanation:
S3 Glacier Deep Archive is the lowest-cost Amazon S3 storage class. It is designed for long-term regulatory archives where retrieval within 12 hours is acceptable. For compliance data that has not been accessed in two years and where cost minimization is the primary goal, it is the correct choice.

**Why it works:** Deep Archive's storage price is the lowest of any S3 class, designed precisely for multi-year retention with infrequent retrieval.

**Why the others don't work:**
- S3 Standard-IA: cheaper than Standard but far more expensive than Deep Archive; faster retrieval than needed.
- S3 Glacier Flexible Retrieval: lower cost than Standard-IA but higher than Deep Archive.
- S3 Intelligent-Tiering: incurs per-object monitoring fees; not the cheapest option for definitively cold data.

skills: 3.6.3: Identifying block storage solutions (for example, Amazon Elastic Block Store [Amazon EBS], instance store).
questions.question:
Management has decided to migrate the company's on-premises Oracle database to an Amazon EC2 instance. The database requires a dedicated block storage volume that can be snapshotted for backups, resized without downtime, and retained if the EC2 instance is replaced during a patching event.

Which storage solution meets all three requirements?

choices.text: Amazon EBS, which provides persistent block storage volumes that support snapshots to Amazon S3, can be modified in size while in use, and persist independently of the EC2 instance lifecycle.
choices.explanation: EBS satisfies all three requirements: it supports point-in-time snapshots, allows volume modifications (including resizing) without detaching, and persists after the instance is terminated or replaced.

choices.text: Instance store, which provides high-throughput block storage directly attached to the host, can be snapshotted using AWS Backup, and persists when the instance is stopped for patching.
choices.explanation: Instance store does not support snapshots and its data is permanently lost when the instance is stopped or terminated, failing both the snapshot and persistence requirements.

choices.text: Amazon S3, which stores the database files as objects, supports versioning as a form of point-in-time backup, and is accessible from any replacement EC2 instance.
choices.explanation: Amazon S3 is object storage. Databases require block-level I/O that S3 does not provide; database files cannot be directly mounted from S3 as a block device.

choices.text: Amazon EFS, which provides a persistent shared file system that can be mounted by a replacement EC2 instance and supports AWS Backup for snapshots.
choices.explanation: Amazon EFS is a file system, not block storage. While it is persistent and supports backups, relational databases that require block-level access typically need EBS, not a shared NFS mount.

questions.tip: Identify the storage type that operates at the block level, persists beyond instance lifecycle, and natively supports point-in-time snapshots.
questions.explanation:
Amazon EBS is the appropriate persistent block storage solution for databases running on EC2. EBS volumes persist independently of the instance lifecycle, support point-in-time snapshots stored in Amazon S3, and can be modified in size or performance tier while attached to a running instance.

**Why it works:** EBS directly addresses all three requirements: snapshot support, live resizing, and persistence after instance replacement.

**Why the others don't work:**
- Instance store: ephemeral; data lost on stop or termination; no snapshot capability.
- Amazon S3: object storage; does not provide block-level I/O required by relational databases.
- Amazon EFS: shared file system (NFS); not block storage; typically not suitable as a primary database volume.

skills: 3.6.3: Identifying block storage solutions (for example, Amazon Elastic Block Store [Amazon EBS], instance store).
questions.question:
The engineering team is comparing Amazon EBS and EC2 instance store for a new high-performance workload. They need to identify characteristics that are TRUE of EC2 instance store volumes.

Which TWO statements correctly describe EC2 instance store?

choices.text: Instance store volumes are physically located on the host server and provide very low-latency, high-throughput block I/O.
choices.explanation: Instance store disks are directly attached to the physical host, giving them lower latency than network-attached EBS volumes, which makes them suitable for temporary high-performance scratch data.

choices.text: Data stored on instance store volumes is lost when the instance is stopped, hibernated, or terminated.
choices.explanation: Instance store is ephemeral. The data does not persist across stop, hibernate, or terminate events, which is a fundamental characteristic that distinguishes it from EBS.

choices.text: Instance store volumes can be detached from one EC2 instance and attached to another within the same Availability Zone.
choices.explanation: Unlike EBS, instance store volumes are not independent network devices. They are fixed to the physical host and cannot be detached and reattached to different instances.

choices.text: Instance store volumes support automated snapshots that are stored in Amazon S3 for point-in-time recovery.
choices.explanation: Instance store does not support snapshots. Only EBS volumes can be snapshotted to Amazon S3.

choices.text: Instance store volumes persist across EC2 instance reboots and retain data as long as the underlying hardware remains healthy.
choices.explanation: While data on an instance store volume does survive a soft reboot of the operating system, it is lost if the instance is stopped or terminated, or if there is a hardware failure on the host.

questions.tip: Consider the physical placement of instance store and what happens to the data when the instance lifecycle changes.
questions.explanation:
EC2 instance store provides block-level storage physically located on the host server, giving it very high throughput and low latency. However, it is entirely ephemeral: data is lost whenever the instance is stopped, hibernated, or terminated.

**Why it works:** Direct physical attachment explains the performance advantage, and the ephemeral nature explains data loss on lifecycle events.

**Why the others don't work:**
- Detaching and reattaching: instance store is bound to the physical host and cannot be moved to another instance like an EBS volume.
- Automated snapshots: only EBS supports snapshots to Amazon S3; instance store has no snapshot capability.
- Persisting across reboots only: while a soft OS reboot retains instance store data, the statement as presented is misleading because data is still lost on stop or termination.

skills: 3.6.4: Identifying file services (for example, Amazon Elastic File System [Amazon EFS], Amazon FSx).
questions.question:
To reduce infrastructure costs, the platform team wants to replace a self-managed NFS server shared by 50 Linux-based EC2 instances across multiple Availability Zones. The replacement solution must scale storage automatically and support standard POSIX file-system permissions.

Which AWS service should they use?

choices.text: Amazon EFS, which provides a fully managed NFS file system that can be mounted concurrently by multiple EC2 instances across Availability Zones and scales storage automatically.
choices.explanation: Amazon EFS is a managed NFS service that grows and shrinks automatically, supports POSIX permissions, and can be mounted by Linux EC2 instances across multiple AZs simultaneously.

choices.text: Amazon EBS Multi-Attach, which allows a single EBS volume to be attached to up to 16 Nitro-based EC2 instances in the same Availability Zone.
choices.explanation: EBS Multi-Attach is limited to 16 instances within a single AZ and requires the application to manage concurrent writes. It does not serve as a general-purpose shared NFS replacement across AZs.

choices.text: Amazon S3, which stores files as objects, provides a flat namespace, and can be mounted on Linux instances using third-party FUSE drivers.
choices.explanation: Amazon S3 is object storage and does not natively provide POSIX semantics or NFS access. Third-party FUSE mounts exist but are not fully POSIX-compliant and are not the recommended managed file service.

choices.text: Amazon FSx for Windows File Server, which provides a fully managed SMB file system optimised for Windows workloads and supports Active Directory integration.
choices.explanation: FSx for Windows File Server uses the SMB protocol and is designed for Windows environments. The workload described uses Linux instances and requires NFS/POSIX, not SMB.

questions.tip: Identify the AWS managed service that provides NFS-compatible shared file access across multiple EC2 instances and Availability Zones.
questions.explanation:
Amazon EFS is a fully managed NFS file system that automatically scales as files are added or removed. It can be mounted concurrently by hundreds of EC2 instances across multiple AZs within a Region and fully supports POSIX file permissions, making it a direct replacement for a self-managed NFS server.

**Why it works:** EFS is purpose-built for shared NFS access on Linux workloads with automatic scaling and multi-AZ mount targets.

**Why the others don't work:**
- EBS Multi-Attach: limited to 16 instances in one AZ; requires application-level concurrency management.
- Amazon S3: object storage without native POSIX/NFS support.
- FSx for Windows File Server: SMB-based; designed for Windows; does not support NFS or standard Linux POSIX permissions.

skills: 3.6.4: Identifying file services (for example, Amazon Elastic File System [Amazon EFS], Amazon FSx).
questions.question:
Following a board decision to migrate all on-premises infrastructure to AWS, the IT team must replace a Windows-based file server used by 200 staff members. The new service must integrate with the company's existing Microsoft Active Directory domain and support the SMB protocol.

Which AWS service is the MOST suitable replacement?

choices.text: Amazon FSx for Windows File Server, which provides a fully managed Windows file system with native SMB support and seamless Microsoft Active Directory integration.
choices.explanation: FSx for Windows File Server is a managed service that natively supports the SMB protocol, integrates with existing Active Directory domains, and is designed as a lift-and-shift replacement for Windows file servers.

choices.text: Amazon EFS, which provides a managed NFS file system that can be mounted by Linux and Windows instances and scales automatically.
choices.explanation: Amazon EFS uses the NFS protocol and is optimised for Linux workloads. While it can be mounted on Windows with additional configuration, it does not natively integrate with Active Directory and is not designed as a Windows SMB file server replacement.

choices.text: Amazon FSx for Lustre, which provides a high-performance parallel file system designed for compute-intensive workloads such as machine learning and high-performance computing.
choices.explanation: FSx for Lustre is a high-performance file system for HPC and data processing workloads. It does not provide SMB access or Active Directory integration for general-purpose Windows file sharing.

choices.text: Amazon S3, which stores files as objects accessible over HTTPS, supports bucket policies for access control, and can be integrated with on-premises Active Directory via AWS IAM Identity Center.
choices.explanation: Amazon S3 is object storage. It does not provide SMB file-sharing capabilities or native Active Directory integration for Windows file server workloads.

questions.tip: Look for the managed file service specifically designed for Windows environments with native protocol and directory service support.
questions.explanation:
Amazon FSx for Windows File Server is a fully managed Windows-native file system that supports the SMB protocol and integrates directly with Microsoft Active Directory. It is designed specifically as a managed replacement for on-premises Windows file servers.

**Why it works:** FSx for Windows File Server provides SMB and Active Directory integration natively, matching both requirements.

**Why the others don't work:**
- Amazon EFS: NFS-based, optimised for Linux; does not natively support SMB or AD integration for Windows file sharing.
- Amazon FSx for Lustre: HPC file system for compute workloads; no SMB or AD integration.
- Amazon S3: object storage accessed via HTTPS; no SMB support.

skills: 3.6.5: Identifying cached file systems (for example, AWS Storage Gateway).
questions.question:
The organization is looking to extend its on-premises file servers to AWS without replacing existing workflows. Users must continue accessing files using their existing NFS and SMB clients, recently accessed data must be available with low latency locally, and the primary copy of all data must be stored durably in Amazon S3.

Which AWS Storage Gateway type meets these requirements?

choices.text: File Gateway, which presents NFS and SMB interfaces to on-premises clients while storing all file data durably in Amazon S3 and caching recently accessed files locally for low-latency reads.
choices.explanation: File Gateway provides NFS and SMB access to on-premises clients, keeps a local cache of recently accessed data for low latency, and stores the full dataset durably in Amazon S3 as the primary storage.

choices.text: Volume Gateway in stored mode, which keeps the entire dataset on-premises as iSCSI block volumes and asynchronously replicates snapshots to Amazon S3 for backup.
choices.explanation: Stored mode Volume Gateway retains the primary dataset on-premises and uploads snapshots to S3. It does not present NFS or SMB interfaces and the primary copy is local, not in S3.

choices.text: Tape Gateway, which emulates a virtual tape library and presents virtual tape drives to on-premises backup software, storing tape data in Amazon S3 and Amazon S3 Glacier.
choices.explanation: Tape Gateway is designed for backup applications using virtual tape library (VTL) interfaces. It does not provide NFS or SMB file access for general-purpose file workloads.

choices.text: Volume Gateway in cached mode, which stores the primary dataset in Amazon S3 and caches frequently accessed blocks locally as iSCSI block volumes presented to on-premises servers.
choices.explanation: Cached mode Volume Gateway stores primary data in S3 and caches hot blocks locally, but it presents an iSCSI block interface, not NFS or SMB file interfaces as required by the scenario.

questions.tip: Identify the gateway type that bridges on-premises file protocols with cloud object storage while keeping hot data accessible locally.
questions.explanation:
AWS Storage Gateway File Gateway translates NFS and SMB file access into Amazon S3 object storage. It maintains a local cache of recently accessed data so on-premises clients experience low-latency reads, while the authoritative copy of all data resides durably in S3. This allows existing file-based workflows to continue without modification.

**Why it works:** File Gateway provides the NFS/SMB interface, local caching, and S3-as-primary-storage combination the scenario requires.

**Why the others don't work:**
- Volume Gateway stored mode: primary data is on-premises; presents iSCSI, not NFS/SMB.
- Tape Gateway: virtual tape library interface for backup software; no file-sharing capability.
- Volume Gateway cached mode: primary data in S3 with local block cache, but uses iSCSI, not NFS or SMB.

skills: 3.6.5: Identifying cached file systems (for example, AWS Storage Gateway).
questions.question:
A manufacturing company has a slow WAN connection to AWS and stores 50 TB of production data in Amazon S3 via AWS Storage Gateway. Operators frequently re-read the same files throughout the day and need those reads to complete quickly despite the limited bandwidth.

Which Storage Gateway feature directly addresses the latency concern?

choices.text: The local cache maintained by the gateway appliance, which stores recently and frequently accessed data on-premises so repeat reads are served locally without traversing the WAN.
choices.explanation: The on-premises cache is the core feature that makes Storage Gateway suitable for low-bandwidth environments. Repeated reads of cached data are served locally, avoiding WAN round trips entirely.

choices.text: Amazon CloudFront, which caches objects at edge locations around the world to reduce the latency of delivering content to users.
choices.explanation: Amazon CloudFront caches content at AWS edge locations for internet-facing distribution. It does not integrate with on-premises Storage Gateway appliances to accelerate local file reads across a WAN.

choices.text: S3 Transfer Acceleration, which uses Amazon CloudFront edge locations to speed up uploads to Amazon S3 from on-premises clients.
choices.explanation: S3 Transfer Acceleration improves upload throughput to S3 by routing data through CloudFront edge locations. It does not help with read latency for data already stored in S3 that is accessed by on-premises users.

choices.text: Amazon ElastiCache, which provides an in-memory caching layer that reduces read latency for database queries and application data.
choices.explanation: Amazon ElastiCache is an in-memory cache for database-driven applications (Redis, Memcached). It is not a component of AWS Storage Gateway and does not accelerate file reads from S3 for on-premises users.

questions.tip: Consider which feature of the gateway appliance itself is responsible for reducing round trips across the WAN for repeated read operations.
questions.explanation:
AWS Storage Gateway maintains a local cache on the gateway appliance. When operators read a file that is already cached, the data is served from local storage without a WAN round trip, dramatically reducing latency. The cache size is configured when deploying the gateway and directly determines how much data can be served locally.

**Why it works:** The on-premises cache eliminates WAN latency for repeated reads of recently accessed files.

**Why the others don't work:**
- Amazon CloudFront: caches objects at internet edge locations for web delivery; not part of Storage Gateway.
- S3 Transfer Acceleration: improves upload speed to S3; does not help with read latency.
- Amazon ElastiCache: in-memory cache for applications; not related to Storage Gateway file access.

skills: 3.6.6: Understanding use cases for lifecycle policies.
questions.question:
You are designing a cost-optimisation strategy for a media company's Amazon S3 bucket. Source video files are accessed daily during editing for 60 days after upload, infrequently reviewed for the following 300 days, and never accessed after one year. The company wants automated storage management with no manual steps after initial configuration.

Which lifecycle policy configuration BEST meets this requirement?

choices.text: Transition objects to S3 Standard-IA at 60 days, transition to S3 Glacier Flexible Retrieval at 360 days, and expire (delete) objects at 365 days.
choices.explanation: This policy matches each phase of the access pattern to the most cost-effective storage class and then deletes objects automatically at the end of the one-year retention period, satisfying all three phases with no ongoing manual work.

choices.text: Transition objects to S3 Glacier Deep Archive at 60 days and expire them at 365 days, eliminating the intermediate Standard-IA tier to simplify the policy.
choices.explanation: Transitioning directly to Glacier Deep Archive at 60 days is too aggressive. Objects still reviewed infrequently during the next 300 days would incur higher retrieval fees and delays from Deep Archive, making it unsuitable for the infrequent-review phase.

choices.text: Enable S3 Intelligent-Tiering on the bucket so objects automatically move between tiers based on access patterns, and set an expiration rule at 365 days.
choices.explanation: S3 Intelligent-Tiering could work for unpredictable patterns but is suboptimal when the access pattern is well-defined and predictable. It also incurs a per-object monitoring fee that adds cost for a pattern that is already known.

choices.text: Keep all objects in S3 Standard for the full year and then use an AWS Lambda function triggered monthly to delete objects older than 365 days.
choices.explanation: Keeping objects in S3 Standard for a full year ignores available cost savings from cheaper tiers. Using Lambda for deletion also introduces operational overhead that lifecycle policies eliminate natively.

questions.tip: Consider matching each distinct phase of the access lifecycle to the storage class best suited for that phase, and include an expiration action to complete the lifecycle.
questions.explanation:
A multi-step lifecycle policy that mirrors the actual access pattern is the most cost-effective approach for a predictable data lifecycle. Transitioning to S3 Standard-IA after the active editing phase, then to Glacier Flexible Retrieval once the infrequent review period begins, and finally expiring objects at one year provides the right tier at each phase without ongoing manual effort.

**Why it works:** Each transition aligns with the defined access phase, and the expiration rule completes the lifecycle automatically.

**Why the others don't work:**
- Deep Archive at 60 days: retrieval from Deep Archive takes hours, making it unsuitable for data still occasionally reviewed.
- Intelligent-Tiering only: adds per-object monitoring fees for a predictable pattern; less cost-effective than explicit rules.
- Stay in Standard plus Lambda: no cost savings from tiering; Lambda-based deletion adds operational complexity.

skills: 3.6.6: Understanding use cases for lifecycle policies.
questions.question:
The operations team is reviewing common use cases for Amazon S3 lifecycle policies before presenting a cost-optimisation proposal to leadership.

Which TWO scenarios represent valid use cases for S3 lifecycle policies?

choices.text: Automatically transitioning database backup files from S3 Standard to S3 Glacier Flexible Retrieval after 90 days to reduce long-term storage costs.
choices.explanation: Transitioning objects to a cheaper storage class after a defined period is a core lifecycle policy use case, directly reducing storage costs for data that ages into infrequent access.

choices.text: Automatically deleting incomplete multipart uploads that have been in progress for more than 7 days to free up storage and avoid unnecessary charges.
choices.explanation: S3 lifecycle policies can include a rule to abort incomplete multipart uploads after a specified number of days, preventing abandoned uploads from consuming storage and accumulating charges.

choices.text: Automatically replicating objects to an S3 bucket in a different AWS Region to meet geographic data residency requirements.
choices.explanation: Geographic replication is handled by S3 Cross-Region Replication, not lifecycle policies. Lifecycle rules manage object transitions and expiration within a bucket, not replication to other regions.

choices.text: Automatically encrypting all new objects uploaded to an S3 bucket using AWS Key Management Service keys.
choices.explanation: Default encryption for a bucket is configured through bucket encryption settings, not lifecycle policies. Lifecycle rules do not manage encryption.

choices.text: Automatically notifying an Amazon SNS topic when an object has existed in the bucket for longer than 30 days.
choices.explanation: Event-driven notifications based on object age are not a lifecycle policy feature. S3 event notifications trigger on object operations (such as creation or deletion), not on elapsed time.

questions.tip: Think about the two types of actions lifecycle policies can perform on objects: storage class transitions and expiration or cleanup actions.
questions.explanation:
Amazon S3 lifecycle policies support two categories of actions: transition actions (moving objects to different storage classes after a specified number of days) and expiration/cleanup actions (deleting objects or aborting incomplete multipart uploads). Transitioning backup files to Glacier and aborting stale multipart uploads are both canonical examples of these two action types.

**Why it works:** Both choices use lifecycle policy actions (transition and abort multipart upload) that are natively supported.

**Why the others don't work:**
- Cross-region replication: a separate S3 feature configured independently of lifecycle rules.
- Default encryption: configured via bucket-level encryption settings, not lifecycle policies.
- SNS notification on age: S3 event notifications fire on object operations, not on time elapsed since upload.

skills: 3.6.7: Understanding use cases for AWS Backup.
questions.question:
Following a board decision on business continuity requirements, the cloud team must ensure that backups of critical Amazon RDS databases and Amazon EFS file systems are stored in a geographically separate AWS Region. The team wants to accomplish this without writing custom automation.

Which AWS Backup capability should they use?

choices.text: Cross-Region copy within a backup plan, which automatically copies recovery points to a specified destination Region on a configured schedule.
choices.explanation: AWS Backup backup plans support a cross-Region copy action that automatically copies recovery points to a secondary Region, satisfying geographic separation requirements without custom scripts or automation.

choices.text: AWS DataSync, which continuously replicates file and object data between AWS storage services across Regions using a managed transfer agent.
choices.explanation: AWS DataSync is a data transfer service for migrating or synchronising data between storage systems. It is not the same as backup; it does not create recovery points or manage backup retention schedules.

choices.text: Amazon S3 Cross-Region Replication, which replicates objects from one S3 bucket to another in a different Region automatically when new objects are uploaded.
choices.explanation: S3 Cross-Region Replication copies S3 objects between buckets. It is specific to Amazon S3 and does not manage RDS or EFS backups through AWS Backup plans.

choices.text: AWS Disaster Recovery Service (AWS DRS), which continuously replicates EC2 instances and on-premises servers to a staging area in a secondary Region for rapid failover.
choices.explanation: AWS Elastic Disaster Recovery (DRS) is designed for server-level continuous replication and failover, not for backup and restore of managed services like RDS and EFS through AWS Backup plans.

questions.tip: Identify the feature within AWS Backup itself that addresses geographic redundancy of recovery points.
questions.explanation:
AWS Backup supports cross-Region copy as part of backup plans. When configured, it automatically copies recovery points to a specified secondary Region after each backup completes. This satisfies geographic separation requirements for disaster recovery without any custom automation.

**Why it works:** Cross-Region copy is a native AWS Backup feature that works for multiple supported services, including RDS and EFS, without custom scripts.

**Why the others don't work:**
- AWS DataSync: data transfer and synchronisation service; does not manage backup plans or recovery points.
- S3 Cross-Region Replication: S3-only; does not manage RDS snapshots or EFS backups.
- AWS DRS: continuous server replication for failover; a different solution from scheduled backup and restore.

skills: 3.6.7: Understanding use cases for AWS Backup.
questions.question: Match each AWS Backup concept to its correct description.

slots.label: Backup plan
Recovery point
Backup vault

choices.text: A policy that defines the backup schedule, retention period, and optional cross-Region copy rules for assigned resources.
choices.explanation: A backup plan in AWS Backup specifies when backups are taken, how long they are kept, and whether they should be copied to another Region.

choices.text: A snapshot or point-in-time copy of a resource created by a completed backup job and stored in a backup vault.
choices.explanation: A recovery point is the actual backup artifact produced by AWS Backup when a backup job completes, representing the state of a resource at a specific point in time.

choices.text: A container that stores and organises recovery points, with configurable access policies and encryption settings.
choices.explanation: A backup vault holds recovery points. It can be locked to prevent deletion, encrypted with a KMS key, and access-controlled via a resource-based policy.

questions.tip: Consider the relationship between the policy that governs backups, the artifact produced, and the storage container that holds it.
questions.explanation: AWS Backup uses three core concepts. A backup plan defines the rules for when and how backups are created. Each completed backup produces a recovery point, which is the actual snapshot stored. Recovery points are held in a backup vault, which is a secure, encrypted container that can be locked to enforce retention compliance.

skills: 3.7.1: Understanding the different AI/ML services and the tasks that they accomplish (for example, Amazon SageMaker, Amazon Lex, Amazon Kendra).
questions.question:
A financial services company is building a customer support portal. They want to add a conversational chatbot that understands natural language questions and routes customers to the correct support topic without requiring them to navigate menus. The solution must understand intent and manage multi-turn dialogue.

Which AWS service is MOST suited for building this conversational interface?

choices.text: Amazon Lex
choices.explanation: Amazon Lex provides automatic speech recognition and natural language understanding to build conversational chatbots with intent recognition and multi-turn dialogue management.

choices.text: Amazon Kendra
choices.explanation: Amazon Kendra is an intelligent enterprise search service. It can retrieve answers from documents but does not manage multi-turn conversational flows or intent routing the way a chatbot framework does.

choices.text: Amazon Polly
choices.explanation: Amazon Polly is a text-to-speech service that converts text into lifelike speech. It does not provide natural language understanding, intent detection, or dialogue management.

choices.text: Amazon Transcribe
choices.explanation: Amazon Transcribe converts audio to text. It handles speech-to-text conversion but does not interpret intent or manage conversational logic.

questions.tip: Focus on which service is specifically designed to understand user intent and conduct multi-turn conversations.
questions.explanation:
Amazon Lex is the AWS service for building conversational interfaces. It powers intent recognition, slot filling, and multi-turn dialogue, which are the core requirements for a natural language chatbot.

**Why it works:** Lex uses the same deep learning technology as Alexa, providing both automatic speech recognition and natural language understanding in a fully managed chatbot framework.

**Why the others don't work:**
- Amazon Kendra: An enterprise search service that retrieves answers from indexed documents; it does not handle conversational dialogue flows.
- Amazon Polly: Synthesizes speech from text; it is an output service with no understanding of user intent.
- Amazon Transcribe: Transcribes spoken audio to text; it provides transcription only, not conversational logic.

skills: 3.7.1: Understanding the different AI/ML services and the tasks that they accomplish (for example, Amazon SageMaker, Amazon Lex, Amazon Kendra).
questions.question: Match each AWS AI/ML service to its primary task.

slots.label: Amazon Rekognition
Amazon Kendra
Amazon Forecast
Amazon Textract

choices.text: Generate time-series predictions from historical data
choices.explanation: Amazon Forecast uses machine learning to produce accurate time-series forecasts such as demand or inventory predictions.

choices.text: Detect objects, faces, and scenes in images and video
choices.explanation: Amazon Rekognition analyzes images and video to identify objects, people, text, scenes, and activities.

choices.text: Extract text and structured data from scanned documents
choices.explanation: Amazon Textract uses ML to read and extract printed text, handwriting, forms, and tables from documents.

choices.text: Search enterprise content using natural language queries
choices.explanation: Amazon Kendra is an intelligent search service that uses NLP to return accurate answers from internal documents and knowledge bases.

questions.tip: Consider the specific data type each service operates on: images, documents, time-series data, or enterprise text repositories.
questions.explanation: Each AWS AI service is optimized for a distinct data type and task. Rekognition handles image and video analysis. Kendra provides intelligent search over enterprise content. Forecast produces time-series predictions. Textract extracts structured data from scanned documents.

skills: 3.7.2: Identifying the services for data analytics (for example, Amazon Athena, Amazon Kinesis, AWS Glue, Amazon QuickSight).
questions.question:
Management has decided to provide business stakeholders with interactive dashboards showing sales trends, regional performance, and inventory levels sourced from the company's data warehouse. The dashboards must be shareable across the organization without requiring stakeholders to write any code or SQL.

Which AWS service is MOST appropriate for creating and publishing these business intelligence dashboards?

choices.text: Amazon QuickSight
choices.explanation: Amazon QuickSight is a fully managed business intelligence service that lets users create interactive visualizations and dashboards from multiple data sources and share them with stakeholders without any coding.

choices.text: Amazon Athena
choices.explanation: Amazon Athena runs SQL queries against data in Amazon S3 but does not provide a visualization or dashboard layer for non-technical business users to consume reports interactively.

choices.text: AWS Glue
choices.explanation: AWS Glue is an ETL and data integration service. It prepares and moves data but does not offer any dashboard or visualization capability for business stakeholders.

choices.text: Amazon Kinesis Data Firehose
choices.explanation: Amazon Kinesis Data Firehose delivers streaming data to destinations like S3 or Redshift. It is a data delivery service, not a business intelligence or dashboard tool.

questions.tip: Think about which service is built for non-technical users to explore data visually and share findings as dashboards.
questions.explanation:
Amazon QuickSight is AWS's managed business intelligence and dashboard service, making it the best fit for creating shareable, interactive visualizations without any code.

**Why it works:** QuickSight connects to data sources including Redshift, S3, Athena, and RDS, and provides a point-and-click interface for building charts, graphs, and dashboards that can be published to named users or groups.

**Why the others don't work:**
- Amazon Athena: A query engine; it produces tabular results, not visual dashboards, and requires SQL knowledge.
- AWS Glue: An ETL service; it has no visualization output for business stakeholders.
- Amazon Kinesis Data Firehose: A streaming data delivery pipeline; it routes data to storage or analytics destinations but does not create dashboards.

skills: 3.7.2: Identifying the services for data analytics (for example, Amazon Athena, Amazon Kinesis, AWS Glue, Amazon QuickSight).
questions.question:
You are designing a data pipeline for an e-commerce platform. Clickstream events are generated continuously from the website and must be ingested in real time, then transformed and cataloged so that analysts can run SQL queries on the processed data in Amazon S3.

Which TWO AWS services should be combined to build this pipeline?

choices.text: Amazon Kinesis Data Firehose to ingest and deliver the real-time clickstream events to Amazon S3
choices.explanation: Amazon Kinesis Data Firehose captures streaming data and delivers it reliably to destinations such as Amazon S3, handling batching and format conversion automatically.

choices.text: AWS Glue to discover, catalog, and transform the data landed in Amazon S3 so analysts can query it with standard SQL
choices.explanation: AWS Glue crawls data in S3 to build a Data Catalog and runs ETL jobs to clean and transform the data, making it queryable by services such as Amazon Athena.

choices.text: Amazon QuickSight to ingest the raw clickstream events and store them durably in Amazon S3 for downstream processing
choices.explanation: Amazon QuickSight is a business intelligence and visualization service. It does not ingest or store raw streaming event data.

choices.text: Amazon SageMaker to catalog and transform the clickstream events into a structured format before querying
choices.explanation: Amazon SageMaker is a machine learning platform. While it can process data, it is not the purpose-built service for ETL cataloging and transformation in a data analytics pipeline.

choices.text: Amazon Rekognition to parse and structure the incoming clickstream event records for storage in Amazon S3
choices.explanation: Amazon Rekognition is an image and video analysis service. It cannot parse or structure text-based clickstream event records.

questions.tip: One service handles continuous real-time data ingestion and delivery; the other handles metadata cataloging and data transformation for downstream queries.
questions.explanation:
The pipeline requires two complementary services: one to capture streaming events and land them in S3, and one to catalog and transform that data so it is queryable.

**Why they work:** Kinesis Data Firehose is a fully managed streaming delivery service that requires no ongoing administration and integrates natively with S3. AWS Glue then crawls the landed data to populate a Data Catalog and can run ETL jobs to partition, convert, or enrich records, enabling Amazon Athena to run fast SQL queries.

**Why the others don't work:**
- Amazon QuickSight: A visualization tool for consuming processed data; it does not ingest raw streaming events.
- Amazon SageMaker: An ML training and inference platform; it is not the standard service for ETL cataloging in analytics pipelines.
- Amazon Rekognition: An image and video AI service; it has no capability to parse structured event data.

skills: 3.8.1: Choosing the appropriate service to deliver messages and to send alerts and notifications.
questions.question:
The operations team needs to send alert notifications to multiple subscriber endpoints simultaneously whenever an Amazon CloudWatch alarm transitions to the ALARM state. Subscribers include an email distribution list, an SMS number, and a webhook endpoint for an internal ticketing system. The team wants a single publish action to fan out to all three endpoints.

Which AWS service BEST meets this requirement?

choices.text: Amazon SNS, configured with three subscriptions on a single topic covering email, SMS, and HTTPS protocols
choices.explanation: Amazon SNS is a pub/sub service that supports multiple simultaneous subscribers across protocols including email, SMS, and HTTPS. A single publish to the topic delivers to all three endpoints at once.

choices.text: Amazon SQS, configured with three separate queues polled by individual Lambda functions that forward messages to each endpoint
choices.explanation: Amazon SQS is a point-to-point queue, not a fan-out pub/sub service. Using three separate queues with Lambda pollers adds significant overhead and does not natively fan out from a single publish.

choices.text: Amazon SES, configured with a rule set that delivers to email, SMS, and webhook targets using a single send action
choices.explanation: Amazon SES is designed for high-volume email delivery and does not natively deliver to SMS or HTTPS webhook endpoints.

choices.text: Amazon EventBridge, configured with a single event bus rule that routes events to three separate targets using a content-based filter
choices.explanation: Amazon EventBridge can route to multiple targets but is event-driven and optimized for service integration, not for delivering human-facing alerts to email and SMS subscribers via a simple pub/sub topic.

questions.tip: Consider which service is purpose-built for delivering a single message to multiple heterogeneous endpoints simultaneously.
questions.explanation:
Amazon SNS is the correct choice because it is a fully managed pub/sub messaging service that supports fan-out delivery to multiple subscribers across different protocols, including email, SMS, and HTTPS, from a single publish action.

**Why it works:** SNS topics allow multiple subscriptions with different protocol types. When a message is published, SNS delivers it to every active subscription concurrently, making it ideal for multi-channel alert notifications.

**Why the others don't work:**
- Amazon SQS: SQS is a point-to-point queue, not a pub/sub fan-out service; a message placed in a queue is consumed by one consumer, not broadcast to many.
- Amazon SES: SES handles high-volume transactional email only and has no native support for SMS or HTTPS webhook delivery.
- Amazon EventBridge: EventBridge is an event bus for service-to-service routing. While it can target multiple destinations, it is not the purpose-built tool for human-facing alert fan-out to email and SMS subscribers.

skills: 3.8.1: Choosing the appropriate service to deliver messages and to send alerts and notifications.
questions.question:
To reduce infrastructure costs, the marketing team is migrating their bulk promotional email campaigns off a third-party email service provider. They send up to two million emails per day and require delivery statistics such as bounces, complaints, and open rates to be tracked. The team uses custom sending domains and needs DKIM signing support.

Which AWS service should they use?

choices.text: Amazon SES, configured with a verified sending domain, DKIM signing enabled, and SNS-based event destinations for bounce and complaint notifications
choices.explanation: Amazon SES is purpose-built for high-volume email sending with built-in DKIM signing, custom domain verification, and event publishing to SNS for bounce, complaint, and delivery tracking.

choices.text: Amazon SNS, configured with an email subscription and a custom sender address to deliver promotional content at scale
choices.explanation: Amazon SNS email subscriptions are intended for notifications to opt-in subscribers, not bulk marketing campaigns. SNS does not support DKIM signing, custom sending domains, or per-message delivery analytics.

choices.text: Amazon Pinpoint, configured as a standalone email channel to send two million promotional emails per day with full bounce and complaint tracking
choices.explanation: Amazon Pinpoint can send email and does track engagement, but it is an end-to-end customer engagement platform oriented toward campaigns and journeys. For raw bulk email infrastructure with DKIM and event data, Amazon SES is the foundational service Pinpoint itself uses under the hood.

choices.text: Amazon Connect, configured with an outbound campaign to send emails to the customer list at high volume with delivery tracking
choices.explanation: Amazon Connect is a cloud contact center service focused on voice and chat interactions, not bulk email delivery. It does not provide an email sending infrastructure for marketing campaigns.

questions.tip: Think about which service is specifically designed for high-volume transactional and marketing email with deliverability controls.
questions.explanation:
Amazon SES is the correct answer because it is purpose-built for high-volume email sending, supporting DKIM signing, custom verified domains, and event publishing to track bounces, complaints, and deliveries at scale.

**Why it works:** SES provides an SMTP interface and API for bulk sends, supports custom domain verification, enables DKIM, and can publish delivery events to Amazon SNS for bounce and complaint processing.

**Why the others don't work:**
- Amazon SNS: SNS email subscriptions are for simple opt-in notification delivery, not bulk marketing. There is no DKIM support or per-message analytics.
- Amazon Pinpoint: Pinpoint is a higher-level engagement platform that uses SES as its email backend. It is better suited for targeted campaign orchestration rather than raw bulk email infrastructure.
- Amazon Connect: Connect is a contact center service for voice and chat, with no capability for bulk email delivery.

skills: 3.8.2: Choosing the appropriate service to meet business application needs.
questions.question:
Management has decided to consolidate the company's communication tools onto AWS. The organization requires video conferencing, team messaging, and screen sharing for internal meetings, with support for dial-in access via a phone number. The solution must be a managed AWS service with no hardware to maintain.

Which service should the team select?

choices.text: Amazon Chime, which provides managed video meetings, team chat, screen sharing, and phone dial-in as a fully managed communications service
choices.explanation: Amazon Chime is a managed business communications service that includes HD video conferencing, team messaging, screen sharing, and dial-in phone access under a single service, with no hardware required.

choices.text: Amazon Connect, configured with a softphone for agents and a shared meeting space accessible to all employees for video conferencing
choices.explanation: Amazon Connect is a cloud contact center service for customer-facing voice and chat interactions. It is not designed for internal team video conferencing or general-purpose meeting collaboration.

choices.text: Amazon WorkMail, configured with integrated calendar invitations and video links to coordinate and host team meetings
choices.explanation: Amazon WorkMail is a managed business email and calendar service. While it can send calendar invitations, it does not provide video conferencing, screen sharing, or phone dial-in capabilities.

choices.text: AWS AppSync, deployed with a real-time WebSocket API to build a custom video conferencing and messaging solution for internal use
choices.explanation: AWS AppSync is a managed GraphQL service for building real-time APIs. It would require significant custom development to deliver video conferencing and team chat, and is not a ready-made communications solution.

questions.tip: Consider which AWS service is built to replace or replicate a business communications platform for meetings and messaging.
questions.explanation:
Amazon Chime is the correct answer because it is a fully managed business communications service that covers video meetings, team messaging, screen sharing, and dial-in phone access with no infrastructure to manage.

**Why it works:** Chime bundles all the required communication features into a single managed service, satisfying the video conferencing, messaging, screen sharing, and dial-in requirements.

**Why the others don't work:**
- Amazon Connect: A customer contact center service, not an internal team communications platform.
- Amazon WorkMail: An email and calendar service only, with no video or screen sharing features.
- AWS AppSync: A GraphQL API service; building video conferencing from scratch would require extensive custom development.

skills: 3.8.2: Choosing the appropriate service to meet business application needs.
questions.question:
The organization is looking to replace two separate third-party subscriptions: a business email and calendar service, and an internal document collaboration platform. Both replacements must be fully managed AWS services that require no on-premises infrastructure and integrate with Microsoft Active Directory for user authentication.

Which TWO AWS services should the team select to fulfill these two requirements?

choices.text: Amazon WorkMail to provide managed business email, shared calendars, and Active Directory integration for the email and calendar replacement
choices.explanation: Amazon WorkMail is a managed email and calendar service that supports Active Directory integration and requires no on-premises infrastructure.

choices.text: Amazon WorkDocs to provide managed document storage, co-authoring, and commenting with Active Directory integration for the document collaboration replacement
choices.explanation: Amazon WorkDocs is a managed document collaboration service that integrates with Microsoft Active Directory for user authentication and requires no on-premises infrastructure.

choices.text: Amazon SES to handle inbound and outbound business email delivery with shared calendar functionality via calendar event attachments
choices.explanation: Amazon SES is a high-volume email sending and receiving service. It does not provide shared calendars, user mailboxes, or document collaboration features.

choices.text: Amazon Connect to provide voice and chat-based communication channels as a replacement for the business email service
choices.explanation: Amazon Connect is a contact center service for customer interactions. It does not provide employee email, calendar, or document collaboration features.

choices.text: Amazon Chime to replace the document collaboration platform by using its team messaging channels for file sharing and threaded discussions
choices.explanation: Amazon Chime provides team messaging with some file sharing, but it is not a dedicated document collaboration platform with co-authoring and version control comparable to WorkDocs.

questions.tip: Match each requirement to the AWS service that is specifically designed to fulfill that category of business application.
questions.explanation:
Amazon WorkMail and Amazon WorkDocs are the correct pair. WorkMail replaces the business email and calendar service, and WorkDocs replaces the document collaboration platform. Both integrate with Microsoft Active Directory and are fully managed.

**Why they work:** WorkMail provides user mailboxes, shared calendars, and AD integration. WorkDocs provides document storage, co-authoring, commenting, and AD integration.

**Why the others don't work:**
- Amazon SES: An email sending service with no calendar or mailbox management for end users.
- Amazon Connect: A contact center service, not an employee productivity or email application.
- Amazon Chime: A meetings and messaging service; while it supports some file sharing, it is not a replacement for a dedicated document collaboration platform.

skills: 3.8.3: Choosing the appropriate service for AWS customer support.
questions.question:
You are managing a production workload that has just experienced an unexpected service degradation. The application team needs to speak directly with an AWS support engineer to diagnose the root cause and restore service as quickly as possible. Your account is enrolled in the Business Support plan.

Which AWS capability should the team use to initiate this interaction?

choices.text: Open a support case in the AWS Support Center and select the phone channel, which is available to Business Support plan customers for production system impairments
choices.explanation: AWS Support Center is where customers open support cases. Business Support includes 24/7 phone access for production system impairments, allowing direct conversation with a support engineer.

choices.text: Use AWS Trusted Advisor to run a real-time check against the affected resources and follow the remediation guidance provided in the recommendations panel
choices.explanation: AWS Trusted Advisor provides automated best-practice checks and recommendations but does not connect customers with live support engineers. It cannot diagnose an active production incident in real time.

choices.text: Open the AWS Health Dashboard and subscribe to a support event notification to track the incident and receive restoration updates from AWS
choices.explanation: AWS Health provides notifications about AWS service events and account-specific health data but does not provide a channel to speak with a support engineer about a specific application-level incident.

choices.text: Use AWS IQ to post a project request and engage an AWS-certified third-party expert to diagnose the production degradation remotely
choices.explanation: AWS IQ connects customers with AWS-certified independent consultants for project-based engagements. It is not the mechanism for opening an urgent support case with AWS support engineers during an active production incident.

questions.tip: Think about which AWS mechanism provides direct access to AWS support engineers for urgent production issues.
questions.explanation:
Opening a support case in AWS Support Center is the correct approach. Business Support includes 24/7 access to AWS support engineers via phone for production system impairments.

**Why it works:** AWS Support Center is the official channel for interacting with AWS support staff. The Business plan tier grants phone access for production issues, enabling direct, real-time troubleshooting.

**Why the others don't work:**
- AWS Trusted Advisor: Provides automated advisory checks, not live support interaction.
- AWS Health Dashboard: Monitors AWS service health and sends account-specific notifications; it is not a support engagement channel.
- AWS IQ: Connects customers with independent certified consultants, not AWS support engineers, and is not suited for emergency incident response.

skills: 3.8.3: Choosing the appropriate service for AWS customer support.
questions.question:
The engineering team is evaluating AWS services to find a community-driven resource where developers can post technical questions about AWS services, search existing answers from AWS experts and certified community members, and get guidance without opening a formal support case.

Which AWS resource BEST meets this need?

choices.text: AWS re:Post, which is a community Q&A service staffed by AWS experts and community contributors where developers can ask and search technical questions
choices.explanation: AWS re:Post is a managed community Q&A forum where developers can post questions and search existing answers. It is staffed by AWS employees and community experts and does not require a formal support plan.

choices.text: AWS Support Center, accessed under the Developer Support plan, which provides a community forum feature alongside case-based support for technical questions
choices.explanation: AWS Support Center is for opening individual support cases with AWS support engineers. It does not have a community forum feature; support cases are private interactions, not searchable community posts.

choices.text: AWS Trusted Advisor, which surfaces community-sourced best-practice recommendations for services the team is currently using based on account configuration
choices.explanation: AWS Trusted Advisor provides automated checks based on account configuration. It is not a community forum and does not surface community-sourced answers to developer questions.

choices.text: AWS IQ, which provides a community marketplace where developers can browse answers posted by certified AWS professionals at no initial cost
choices.explanation: AWS IQ is a marketplace for engaging certified AWS professionals on paid project engagements. It is not a community Q&A forum for searching and posting technical questions.

questions.tip: Consider which AWS resource is specifically designed for community-based technical question and answer interactions.
questions.explanation:
AWS re:Post is the correct answer because it is AWS's official community Q&A service where developers can post technical questions, search prior answers, and receive responses from AWS employees and community experts without a formal support case.

**Why it works:** re:Post replaces the older AWS Forums and provides a searchable, community-moderated knowledge base available to all AWS users.

**Why the others don't work:**
- AWS Support Center: Used for private, individual support cases, not community discussions.
- AWS Trusted Advisor: Provides automated best-practice checks, not community Q&A.
- AWS IQ: A marketplace for paid professional engagements, not a community question forum.

skills: 3.8.3: Choosing the appropriate service for AWS customer support.
questions.question: Match each customer support scenario to the AWS resource that BEST addresses it.

slots.label: A startup wants to search existing community answers to a technical question about Amazon RDS without opening a support case
A company needs a certified AWS professional to help architect a new data lake solution as a short-term paid engagement
An enterprise customer requires 24/7 direct access to senior AWS engineers with a 15-minute response time for critical system failures

choices.text: AWS re:Post community Q&A forum
choices.explanation: AWS re:Post provides a searchable, community-driven Q&A service for technical questions without requiring a support plan or opening a case.

choices.text: AWS IQ certified professional marketplace
choices.explanation: AWS IQ connects customers with certified independent AWS professionals for project-based or consulting engagements.

choices.text: AWS Enterprise Support plan with a Technical Account Manager
choices.explanation: AWS Enterprise Support provides 24/7 access to senior support engineers, a 15-minute response SLA for critical issues, and a dedicated Technical Account Manager.

questions.tip: Consider whether the scenario requires community knowledge sharing, professional project help, or direct access to AWS support engineers under a paid plan.
questions.explanation: AWS re:Post is a community Q&A forum suitable for self-service technical questions. AWS IQ connects customers with certified consultants for project engagements. AWS Enterprise Support provides the highest tier of direct AWS engineering access, including a 15-minute SLA for business-critical failures.

skills: 3.8.4: Choosing the appropriate option for business support assistance.
questions.question:
After reviewing quarterly spending, a medium-sized e-commerce company is evaluating AWS Support plan options. Their workloads are all in production, and they need access to AWS support engineers via phone and chat with a response time of no more than four hours for production system impairments.
